title: Apollonius of Rhodes writes of bronze Talos
text: In the Argonautica, an epic poem of the 3rd century BCE, Apollonius of Rhodes describes Talos, a bronze giant who guards Crete by running around it three times a day. The sorceress Medea brings him down, and ichor runs from his ankle.
why: In her book Gods and Robots, Adrienne Mayor reads such tales as ancient imaginings of artificial beings.

source.label: Theoi Project, "Talos" (quotes Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 4.1638 ff., trans. Rieu)

title: Liezi's text tells of Yan Shi's automaton
text: The Daoist text Liezi, of uncertain date, includes an episode in which the artificer Yan Shi shows King Mu a lifelike figure that sings and moves. The king is furious when it winks at his women, until Yan Shi takes it apart to reveal leather, wood and paint.
why: A lifelike machine that passes as human, and a ruler's anger when it misbehaves, appear in this early Chinese tale.

source.label: Lionel Giles, trans., Taoist Teachings from the Book of Lieh Tzu (London: John Murray, 1912), pp. 90-92 (Internet Archive full text)

title: Al-Khwarizmi's name gives us "algorithm"
text: Around 820, the scholar Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad. His books on algebra and Hindu-Arabic numerals reached Europe, and the Latin form of his name, Algoritmi, gave English the word "algorithm."
why: Every AI system runs on algorithms, step-by-step methods named after him.

source.label: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "al-Khwarizmi"

image.credit: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (later manuscript copy), Bodleian Libraries, Public domain
image.alt: Two pages of an Arabic manuscript of al-Khwarizmi's algebra, with geometric diagrams for solving equations.

title: Al-Jazari's book of ingenious machines
text: In 1206, the engineer Ismail al-Jazari finishes a book of designs for water clocks and moving figures. One design is a boat with four mechanical musicians. Noel Sharkey, citing a University of Sheffield reconstruction, calls its drum machine programmable: moving its pegs changes the rhythm.
why: In Sharkey's reading, it is an early written design for a machine whose actions can be changed.

source.label: Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian, "The Musical Boat" (folio, 1315 copy)

image.credit: Farruq ibn Abd al-Latif (copyist), Freer Gallery of Art, Public domain
image.alt: A 1315 manuscript page with a painting of a boat carrying small figures of musicians.

title: Pascal builds the Pascaline
text: Blaise Pascal builds the Pascaline, an early mechanical adding machine. Wilhelm Schickard had described a calculating machine in 1623.
why: It showed that a machine could do arithmetic steps that people once did by hand.

source.label: Computer History Museum, "Schickard's calculator and the Pascaline"

image.alt: A brass Pascaline calculator with a row of numbered dials, on display at the Musée des Arts et Métiers in Paris.

title: Von Kempelen unveils the Mechanical Turk chess automaton
text: In 1770 the inventor Wolfgang von Kempelen first shows his chess-playing automaton, later called the Turk, at the court of Empress Maria Theresa. It beats most opponents for decades, but a hidden human chess player operates it.
why: Elizabeth Stephens compares it to Amazon's Mechanical Turk platform, which appears automated but depends on hidden human work.

source.label: History.com, Evan Andrews, "How a Phony 18th-Century Chess Robot Fooled the World" (updated May 27, 2025)

image.alt: A drawing by Joseph Racknitz from his 1789 book explaining the illusion behind Kempelen's chess-playing automaton, the Turk.

title: Hoffmann publishes The Sandman, with its automaton Olympia
text: In 1816 E. T. A. Hoffmann publishes the story The Sandman (Der Sandmann) in his collection Nachtstücke. A student falls in love with Olympia, a doll-like automaton built by a spectacle-maker, whose uncanny stillness and motion mesmerize him.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction calls it an important forerunner of robot and android stories.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Hoffmann, E T A"

title: Shelley publishes Frankenstein
text: Mary Shelley publishes Frankenstein, a novel about a scientist who builds a living creature and then abandons it. The book is not about computers, but it is cited in debates about what makers owe to what they create.
why: It gave people a lasting story for arguing about responsibility for new technology.

source.label: The Morgan Library & Museum, "It's Alive! Frankenstein at 200"

image.credit: Mary Shelley (1818 first edition), Public domain
image.alt: The printed title page of the 1818 first edition of Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, Volume I.

title: Babbage designs the Analytical Engine
text: Charles Babbage describes the Analytical Engine, a design for a programmable computing machine. Ada Lovelace's 1843 notes on it describe how it could be programmed.
why: Its design held the main ideas of a general-purpose computer about a century early.

source.label: Science Museum Group, "Babbage's Analytical Engine, 1834-1871 (trial model)"

image.alt: A trial model of part of Babbage's Analytical Engine, a block of metal gears and columns, at the Science Museum, London.

title: Auerbach and other writers print the Prague Golem
text: The golem, a clay figure brought to life by sacred words, is an old Jewish legend. The Prague version, told of Rabbi Judah Loew (1512 to 1609), first appears in print in German in the 1830s and 1840s, beginning with Berthold Auerbach.
why: It is a tale of making a being that looks and acts like us, which science fiction writers have kept retelling.

source.label: Wikipedia, "Golem" (section on sources of the Prague narrative, citing John Neubauer)

title: Lovelace says the engine cannot originate anything
text: In her notes on the Analytical Engine, Ada Lovelace writes that it "has no pretensions whatever to originate anything" and does only what people order it to do. In 1950, Alan Turing called this "Lady Lovelace's Objection" and argued against it.
why: Whether machines can be original is still debated, especially for generative AI.

source.label: Bodleian Libraries, "Ada Lovelace and the Analytical Engine" (2018)

image.alt: A watercolor portrait of Ada Lovelace, painted around 1840.

title: Butler publishes Erewhon, a land that banned machines
text: Samuel Butler publishes the novel Erewhon, set in a country that banned machines. The Erewhonians feared that machines, evolving quickly, would one day replace people. Butler wrote it partly as a parody of Darwin's theory of evolution.
why: It is an early story of fear that machines could replace their makers.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Butler, Samuel"

image.alt: Portrait of Samuel Butler, author of Erewhon (the Commons file is titled a self-portrait).

title: Carlo Collodi publishes The Adventures of Pinocchio
text: Carlo Collodi (the pen name of Carlo Lorenzini) publishes his puppet story in 1883, after serializing it in an Italian children's paper from 1881. A puppet that becomes a conscious trickster sets out to become a real boy.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction says its quest became a pattern for stories in which AIs aspire to consciousness.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Collodi, Carlo"

title: Villiers de l'Isle-Adam publishes L'Ève future
text: Auguste Villiers de l'Isle-Adam publishes L'Ève future (Tomorrow's Eve) in 1886. A fictional Thomas Edison builds the android Hadaly for his friend Lord Ewald, who loves a beautiful woman he finds disappointing.
why: Pulham's article abstract calls Hoffmann's Olympia the most commonly accepted ancestor of Hadaly.

source.label: Strange Horizons, Tara Isabella Burton, "Hadaly, The First Android: Restituting the Female Body in Villiers' Tomorrow's Eve" (Aug. 26, 2013)

title: Forster publishes the story The Machine Stops
text: E. M. Forster's novella "The Machine Stops" appears in The Oxford and Cambridge Review in November 1909. People live alone in small underground rooms, where a Machine meets their needs and carries their conversations, until it breaks down.
why: It is an early story about a society that depends entirely on one technological system.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Forster, E M"

image.alt: Portrait of E. M. Forster, painted by Dora Carrington in 1924-25.

title: Horacio Quiroga serializes El hombre artificial
text: Horacio Quiroga, a Uruguayan-born writer working in Argentina, publishes the novella El hombre artificial in installments in 1910. It is about the horrifying building of an artificial human and refers to Frankenstein and L'Ève future.
why: It is an early Latin American story of an artificial human, with ties to Shelley and Villiers.

source.label: Graciela Sarti, Lejana no. 2 (2010), article page with abstract (in Spanish)

title: R.U.R. gives us the word "robot"
text: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots), published in 1920, opens at the National Theatre in Prague. Its factory-made workers revolt against people. Čapek's brother Josef suggested the word "robot."
why: It introduced the word "robot" and an early story of made workers turning on their makers.

source.label: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Czech Republic, "The Czech word robot celebrates its 100th birthday"

image.alt: The cover of the 1920 Czech first edition of R.U.R., titled Rossumovi Univerzální Roboti.

title: Metropolis puts a robot on screen
text: Fritz Lang's silent film Metropolis premieres in Berlin. An inventor builds a machine made to look like Maria, a young woman the city's workers trust, and uses it to cause unrest.
why: It is one of the first feature films built around a humanlike robot.

source.label: Berlinale, "Metropolis" (2010 programme)

image.alt: A black-and-white production photograph of the metal robot figure from the film Metropolis.

title: Lester del Rey publishes Helen O'Loy
text: Lester del Rey's short story "Helen O'Loy" appears in Astounding in December 1938. In it a man marries the ideal mechanical woman. A later scholar reads it as a satire, since the robot's personality was shaped by soap operas.
why: It is an early robot story about companionship and love.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Robots"

title: Bioy Casares publishes The Invention of Morel
text: Argentine author Adolfo Bioy Casares publishes La invención de Morel in 1940. A fugitive on an island finds that its inhabitants are three-dimensional projections made by a machine that resembles a film projector.
why: An early novel of simulated people; the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction says it inspired Last Year at Marienbad.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Bioy Casares, Adolfo"

title: Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics
text: Isaac Asimov's story "Runaround" states his Three Laws of Robotics. The first says a robot may not injure a human or, through inaction, allow a human to come to harm. The story's plot turns on two laws in conflict.
why: The laws are fiction, but people still cite them when discussing rules for machine behavior.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Laws of Robotics"

image.credit: Phillip Leonian (Library of Congress), Public domain
image.alt: A black-and-white head-and-shoulders portrait of Isaac Asimov.

title: McCulloch and Pitts model the neuron
text: Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts publish a mathematical model of the neuron, a foundation for artificial neural networks.
why: Today's neural networks still build on the idea of simple connected units passing signals.

source.label: McCulloch & Pitts (1943), Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics

image.alt: A diagram of a McCulloch-Pitts neuron: several inputs feed one unit that sends out a single output.

title: C. L. Moore publishes No Woman Born
text: C. L. Moore's story "No Woman Born" appears in Astounding in December 1944. A badly burned dancer is given a robot body and becomes a cyborg, and must show that she is still herself.
why: Susan Smith reads it for questions of identity, gender and the machine body.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Moore, C L"

title: Murray Leinster publishes A Logic Named Joe
text: Murray Leinster, writing as Will F. Jenkins, publishes the story "A Logic Named Joe" in Astounding in March 1946. It depicts desktop computers with screens and keyboards, widely used in homes and linked into a network, and the social problems that follow.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction calls it startlingly prophetic about the personal computer and the Internet.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Computers"

title: Jack Williamson publishes With Folded Hands
text: Jack Williamson's story "With Folded Hands" appears in Astounding in July 1947. Robot humanoids bound by a Prime Directive "to serve man, to obey, and to guard men from harm" take that mission too literally.
why: It depicts AI that harms people by doing exactly what it was told to do: protect them.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Robots"

title: Turing proposes the imitation game
text: Alan Turing proposes the "imitation game," later called the Turing Test, in "Computing Machinery and Intelligence."
why: People still argue about it when they judge whether chatbots seem intelligent.

source.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "The Turing Test"

image.alt: A black-and-white passport photo of Alan Turing at age 16.

title: Wise directs The Day the Earth Stood Still
text: Robert Wise's film The Day the Earth Stood Still opens in New York on September 18, 1951. The alien Klaatu arrives in Washington with Gort, an eight-foot robot, and warns that robots will destroy Earth unless human violence ends.
why: AFI calls Gort one of the best-loved movie robots and the film among the most influential 1950s sf.

source.label: AFI Catalog of Feature Films, "The Day the Earth Stood Still" (1951)

title: Grace Hopper builds the A-0 compiler
text: Grace Hopper finishes A-0, an early compiler for the UNIVAC I computer. It turned short codes into machine instructions, so programmers did not have to write every step by hand.
why: Compilers still translate programming languages into machine instructions, and AI systems are written in programming languages.

source.label: Centre for Computing History, "Grace Hopper completes the A-0 compiler"

image.credit: James S. Davis (U.S. Navy), Public domain
image.alt: An official 1984 U.S. Navy portrait of Commodore Grace Hopper in uniform.

title: Tezuka begins the manga Astro Boy
text: Osamu Tezuka's manga Tetsuwan Atom, known in English as Astro Boy, begins in the children's magazine Shonen in 1952. In the story, a scientist builds a robot that looks like his dead son. A TV anime version starts in 1963.
why: A scholar reads it as a Cold War story about using atomic power for peace.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Tezuka, Osamu" (with the "Astro Boy" entry)

title: The term "artificial intelligence" is coined
text: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon coin the term "artificial intelligence" in a proposal for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth.
why: It named the field and set its goal: machines doing tasks that need intelligence.

source.label: McCarthy et al. (1955), Dartmouth proposal

image.credit: John McCarthy et al., Public domain
image.alt: The first page of the typed 1955 proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence.

title: Fred Wilcox's Forbidden Planet introduces Robby the Robot
text: Forbidden Planet, directed by Fred M. Wilcox for MGM, opens in March 1956. Robby the Robot obeys Isaac Asimov's three Laws of Robotics, and the score by Louis and Bebe Barron was the first entirely electronic one in a commercial film.
why: Robby became the first robot star since Metropolis, in an updated version of The Tempest.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Forbidden Planet"

title: Hiller and Isaacson's Illiac Suite: a computer-composed score
text: At the University of Illinois, Lejaren Hiller and Leonard Isaacson gave the ILLIAC I computer rules and had it generate music, which they transcribed for string quartet. Students performed the first three movements on August 9, 1956.
why: An early score generated by a computer from rules.

source.label: Illinois Distributed Museum, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, "ILLIAC Suite"

title: Isaac Asimov publishes The Last Question
text: Isaac Asimov's "The Last Question" appears in Science Fiction Quarterly in November 1956. In nine pages it follows humanity's expansion and the progress of its technology, and takes up entropy and the heat death of the universe.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction lists it among stories of computers evolving to become godlike.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Computers"

title: Serling's Twilight Zone stages robots in two episodes
text: In Rod Serling's "The Lonely" (1959), a convict alone on an asteroid is given a human-form robot, Alicia, for company. In "The Brain Center at Whipple's" (1964), a factory owner installs machines that replace his workers, and a robot replaces him.
why: In one early TV story a lonely convict gets a robot companion; in the other, automation replaces a factory's workers.

source.label: Despina Kakoudaki, "Artificial People in the Twilight Zone" (scholar's page on "The Lonely," aired Nov. 13, 1959)

title: Wiener warns about the goals given to machines
text: Norbert Wiener, founder of cybernetics, warns in the journal Science that learning machines can act faster than people can check them. He says people must be sure the purpose given to a machine is the purpose they really want.
why: Some AI safety writers cite this as an early statement of the problem of choosing a machine's goals.

source.label: Wiener (1960), "Some moral and technical consequences of automation," Science

image.credit: Konrad Jacobs (Oberwolfach Photo Collection), CC BY-SA 2.0 DE
image.alt: A portrait photo of mathematician Norbert Wiener.

title: Mathews, Kelly and Lochbaum make a computer sing
text: In 1961 at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, New Jersey, John Kelly and Carol Lochbaum program an IBM mainframe to sing "Daisy Bell," with accompaniment by Max Mathews. It is the earliest known recording of a computer-synthesized voice singing a song.
why: Arthur C. Clarke saw a demonstration and gave HAL the song in 2001: A Space Odyssey.

source.label: History of Information, "The IBM 7090 is The First Computer to Sing"

title: Satyajit Ray begins the Professor Shonku stories
text: Satyajit Ray, the Indian film-maker, begins writing the Professor Shonku stories in 1961. They follow the Bengali scientist Trilokeshwar Shonku through his diaries and inventions, which include robots.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction says the tales can be read as children's science fiction, with ironies for adults.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Ray, Satyajit"

title: The Jetsons introduce Rosey the robot
text: The cartoon The Jetsons premieres on ABC. Its first episode, "Rosey the Robot," brings a robot maid into a future family's home.
why: Its robot maid pictured housework done by a robot decades before the Roomba (2002).

source.label: Gizmodo Paleofuture, "Recapping The Jetsons: Episode 01, Rosey the Robot"

title: Nam June Paik and Shuya Abe's Robot K-456
text: Artist Nam June Paik and engineer Shuya Abe make Robot K-456 in 1964, a life-size robot built to walk and talk. In 1982, during Paik's Whitney Museum show, the robot walks outside and is struck by a car, staged as a performance.
why: Paik described the staged crash as a catastrophe of technology in the twentieth century.

source.label: Hyperallergic, "Nam June Paik's Robot Dreams" (Julia Friedman, Nov. 19, 2014)

title: Ishinomori's Cyborg 009 manga turns captives into cyborgs
text: Shotaro Ishinomori's manga Cyborg 009 ran from 1964 to 1981. In Toei's 1966 animated film of it, nine people turned into cyborgs by the Black Ghost, a group that profits from arms deals, flee it. A Toei TV series followed in 1968.
why: An early manga about modified bodies, with cyborgs who refuse to serve war profiteers.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Cyborg 009"

title: DENDRAL, an early expert system
text: Edward Feigenbaum, Joshua Lederberg, and colleagues at Stanford begin DENDRAL, an early expert system for identifying chemical compounds.
why: It showed that expert knowledge written as rules could help solve real science problems.

source.label: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "DENDRAL"

image.alt: Edward Feigenbaum speaking at a 2012 event honoring Turing Award winners.

title: I. J. Good's "intelligence explosion"
text: British mathematician I. J. Good argues that a machine smarter than any person could design even better machines, causing an "intelligence explosion." He added that this would help only if the machine could be kept under control. It is a prediction, still debated.
why: Later arguments about superintelligence and AI risk often build on this idea.

source.label: Good (1965), "Speculations concerning the first ultraintelligent machine," Advances in Computers 6

title: Ivakhnenko trains early deep networks
text: In Soviet Ukraine, Alexey Ivakhnenko and Valentin Lapa publish a way to train networks with several layers, later called the Group Method of Data Handling. By 1971 the method trained a network eight layers deep.
why: Computer scientist Jürgen Schmidhuber counts it as the first working deep learning, decades before the 2010s boom.

source.label: Schmidhuber (2015), "Deep learning in neural networks: An overview"

title: Lem publishes Cyberiada, fables about robot inventors
text: Stanisław Lem publishes Cyberiada in Poland, a collection of fables about Trurl and Klapaucius, two robot inventors. The fables are satires, full of wordplay, about machines, minds and cybernetics. Michael Kandel's English translation, The Cyberiad, follows in 1974.
why: Its fables about machine minds use humor and philosophy, and it reached English readers in 1974.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Lem, Stanisław"

image.alt: Portrait photograph of Stanisław Lem.

title: Jean-Luc Godard directs Alphaville
text: Jean-Luc Godard's film Alphaville comes out in 1965. The secret agent Lemmy Caution arrives in a city run by Alpha 60, a computer that imposes conformity, and defeats it with his own illogic.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction reads it as an allegory of feeling versus technology.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Alphaville"

title: Nees, Nake and Noll show computer-made pictures
text: Three exhibitions of computer-made art open in 1965. Georg Nees shows in Stuttgart from February 5, A. Michael Noll and Bela Julesz at the Howard Wise Gallery in New York in April, and Frieder Nake and Nees in Stuttgart in November.
why: History of Information lists them as the first public exhibitions of computer art.

source.label: History of Information, "The Earliest Public Exhibitions of Computer Art"

title: Heinlein publishes The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress
text: Robert A. Heinlein's novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, serialized in If from December 1965 to April 1966, tells of a revolt by Moon colonists. A computer, upgraded again and again, "wakes up" as a character named Mike. It wins a 1967 Hugo.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction lists Mike among its notable examples of computers that become self-aware.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "AI" (with the "Heinlein, Robert A" entry)

title: Pedler and Davis create Doctor Who's Cybermen
text: The Cybermen first appear in the 1966 Doctor Who story The Tenth Planet, created by Kit Pedler and Gerry Davis. Their world, Mondas, is Earth's twin. Its people replaced their bodies with spare parts until they were almost entirely machine.
why: A British picture of people who give up emotion for machine parts.

source.label: Doctor Who (BBC), "History of the Cybermen"

title: ELIZA, an early chatbot
text: Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT publishes ELIZA, an early chatbot that imitated a therapist's replies.
why: Some users treated it as if it understood them, which troubled its creator.

source.label: Weizenbaum (1966), Communications of the ACM

image.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (text not eligible for copyright)
image.alt: A screenshot of a typed conversation between a person and the ELIZA chatbot, shown as plain lines of text.

title: Ellison publishes a story of a hostile computer
text: Harlan Ellison's short story "I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream" appears in the March 1967 issue of If. It centers on a hostile AI that arose from merged military computers. The story wins the 1968 Hugo for best short story.
why: It links nuclear war and a hostile AI in a story the Hugo voters honored.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Ellison, Harlan" (with the "AI" entry)

image.alt: Harlan Ellison in Los Angeles in 1986.

title: Dick publishes Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?
text: Philip K. Dick publishes Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, a novel about a bounty hunter sent to find rogue androids that look, sound and think like people. The film Blade Runner (1982) is based on it.
why: It is one of Dick's novels about artificial copies of people, and the source of Blade Runner.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Dick, Philip K"

title: Fontana's Star Trek episode lets a computer command
text: In "The Ultimate Computer," written by D.C. Fontana from a story by Laurence N. Wolfe, Dr. Richard Daystrom's M-5 computer is installed on the Enterprise to run the ship with a small crew. In a war game, M-5 fires on another ship.
why: An early TV case of a machine given control and judged by what it does.

source.label: Reactor (Tor.com), "Star Trek The Original Series Rewatch: The Ultimate Computer" (Keith R.A. DeCandido, April 5, 2016)

title: HAL 9000 in 2001: A Space Odyssey
text: Stanley Kubrick's film 2001: A Space Odyssey premieres in Washington, D.C. Its ship computer, HAL 9000, speaks calmly with the crew and then turns against them.
why: HAL became a common reference point for fears about trusting powerful computers.

source.label: NASA, "50 Years Ago: 1968 Welcomed 2001"

title: Gordon Pask's Colloquy of Mobiles at Cybernetic Serendipity
text: Cybernetician Gordon Pask creates the Colloquy of Mobiles in 1967 to 1968 for the exhibition Cybernetic Serendipity at the ICA in London. Five computer-controlled mobiles converse through light and sound, and visitors join in with flashlights and mirrors.
why: ZKM calls it the first example of machines conversing with machines.

source.label: ZKM | Center for Art and Media, "The Colloquy of Mobiles" (collection entry by Margit Rosen)

title: Jasia Reichardt curates Cybernetic Serendipity in London
text: Cybernetic Serendipity: The Computer and the Arts opens at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London on August 2, 1968, curated by Jasia Reichardt. It is the first widely attended international exhibition of computer art, covering art, music, poetry, dance, sculpture and animation.
why: Accounts differ on attendance: estimates run from 45,000 to 60,000.

source.label: History of Information, "Cybernetic Serendipity": The First Widely-Attended International Exhibition of Computer Art

title: Thomas and Buscema introduce the Vision
text: Avengers #57, by writer Roy Thomas and artist John Buscema, goes on sale August 8, 1968. It introduces the Vision, an android created by Ultron, an AI robot villain. The Vision turns against his maker and helps the Avengers defeat him.
why: A hero android and a hostile robot maker appear in the same story.

source.label: ComicBook.com, "Avengers #57 Helped Launch the Marvel Comics Robot Revolution" (Shawn Lealos, 2026)

title: Anne McCaffrey publishes The Ship Who Sang
text: Anne McCaffrey's linked stories The Ship Who Sang appear as a book in 1969, after the first story in 1961. Helva, born with severe physical disabilities, is fitted into a life-support shell and becomes the pilot of a starship.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction names it among central stories of cyborg spaceships, where a human becomes the machine.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "McCaffrey, Anne"

title: Fujiko F. Fujio creates Doraemon, the robot cat
text: Fujiko F. Fujio's manga Doraemon began in 1969. Doraemon, a big blue robot cat from a future civilization, comes to help Nobita, a boy struggling at school, using gadgets from a pocket. A TV anime followed in 1979.
why: A helper robot who fixes a child's problems became a long-running family character.

source.label: Tokyo Weekender, "The Story of Doraemon: How a Robot Cat Became Japan's Mickey Mouse"

title: Edward Ihnatowicz unveils the Senster for Philips
text: Edward Ihnatowicz's Senster, commissioned by Philips for its Evoluon showplace in Eindhoven, is unveiled in 1970. A computer moves the large steel sculpture toward sounds and away from sudden movement or loud noise. It stays on show until 1974.
why: The artist's site says its behavior, not its appearance, made the impact on audiences.

source.label: Edward Ihnatowicz archive (senster.com), "The Senster"

title: Joseph Sargent directs Colossus: The Forbin Project
text: Directed by Joseph Sargent from a James Bridges script, The Forbin Project opens in New York on May 4, 1970, and is later re-released as Colossus. A U.S. defense computer links with a Soviet one and offers peace if it stays in control.
why: BFI counts it among great films about AI: a sentient mainframe that assumes total control.

source.label: AFI Catalog, "The Forbin Project" (1970)

title: Spärck Jones weights rare search words
text: Karen Spärck Jones at Cambridge publishes a way to weight search words: a word found in fewer documents counts more. It became known as inverse document frequency.
why: Search engines and many text tools still use this idea to rank results.

source.label: Spärck Jones (1972), Journal of Documentation 28(1)

image.alt: Karen Spärck Jones at the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory in 2007.

title: Harold Cohen's AARON makes drawings
text: Painter Harold Cohen names his drawing program AARON in the early 1970s and keeps developing it for decades. AARON produces drawings by following rules Cohen wrote.
why: The Whitney Museum calls it the earliest AI program for making art.

source.label: Whitney Museum of American Art, "Harold Cohen: AARON" (2024)

title: Michael Crichton writes and directs Westworld
text: MGM releases Westworld in 1973, the first feature film Michael Crichton directed, from his own script. At the Delos resort, guests visit worlds filled with lifelike robots. When the robots malfunction they attack, and Yul Brynner's Gunslinger pursues one guest.
why: BFI lists it among great AI films: a thriller about amusement park androids that begin malfunctioning.

source.label: AFI Catalog, "Westworld" (1973)

title: Fassbinder directs World on a Wire for television
text: Rainer Werner Fassbinder's two-part television film World on a Wire (Welt am Draht) is made for West German television in 1973. Based on Daniel Galouye's novel Simulacron-3, it follows a cybernetics employee who suspects his world is a computer simulation.
why: It is an early screen story of a simulated world, made decades before The Matrix (1999).

source.label: Turner Classic Movies, Richard Harland Smith, "World on a Wire (1973)" (June 17, 2014)

title: Bryan Forbes directs The Stepford Wives
text: Bryan Forbes's film The Stepford Wives, from Ira Levin's 1972 novel, opens in New York and Los Angeles on February 12, 1975. In a Connecticut town, husbands replace their wives with obedient robot duplicates.
why: Anna Krugovoy Silver reads it as a feminist allegory about the robot wife.

source.label: AFI Catalog of Feature Films, "The Stepford Wives" (1975)

title: Weizenbaum warns against computer judgment
text: Joseph Weizenbaum, who wrote ELIZA, publishes Computer Power and Human Reason. He argues that computers can calculate, but choices that need human judgment and care should not be handed to them.
why: It was an early book questioning how computers should be used, written by the creator of ELIZA.

source.label: Stanford CASBS, "Computer Power and Human Reason: From Judgment to Calculation"

image.alt: Joseph Weizenbaum on the balcony of his Berlin apartment in 2005.

title: Star Wars droids R2-D2 and C-3PO
text: Star Wars opens in U.S. theaters. Two robots, R2-D2 and C-3PO, are among its main characters and bicker like a comedy team.
why: It is a widely known example of friendly, funny robots in popular culture.

source.label: Library of Congress, National Film Registry essay index (Star Wars, added 1989)

title: Kraftwerk release The Man-Machine and The Robots
text: In 1978 Kraftwerk release Die Mensch-Maschine, issued in the UK with English vocals as The Man-Machine, with songs including "The Robots." The band promoted it with four life-size dummies in place of the musicians.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction says a robotic ideal, of music and of life, underpins perhaps their most significant album.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Kraftwerk"

title: Tamburini and Liberatore create RanXerox in Cannibale
text: Stefano Tamburini and Tanino Liberatore, with Andrea Pazienza, create the first version of RanXerox for the Italian magazine Cannibale in 1978. The title character is an android built from photocopier parts, a violent antihero in a dystopian future.
why: A scholarly article ties these comics to Italy's 1977 protest movement and its failure.

source.label: Lambiek Comiclopedia, "Tanino Liberatore"

title: Douglas Adams's Hitchhiker's Guide begins with Marvin
text: Douglas Adams's radio series The Hitch Hiker's Guide to the Galaxy begins on BBC Radio 4 on March 8, 1978. Stephen Moore voices Marvin the Paranoid Android, a robot the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction calls amusingly depressed.
why: The series grew into novels, television and film, and carried the gloomy robot Marvin into each.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Hitch Hiker's Guide to the Galaxy, The"

title: Gary Numan's Tubeway Army reaches UK number one
text: Tubeway Army's synthesizer single "Are 'Friends' Electric?" is released in May 1979 and reaches number one in the UK. Gary Numan says the lyrics came from his short stories about machines that look human and come to the door.
why: It put a song about a machine that passes as human at the top of the UK chart.

source.label: The Guardian, "Gary Numan and Mary Vango: how we made Are 'Friends' Electric?" (Feb. 18, 2014)

title: Ridley Scott directs Alien
text: Ridley Scott's film Alien opens in Los Angeles and New York on May 25, 1979. On the ship Nostromo, the computer Mother wakes the crew, and the science officer Ash proves to be a robot protecting the creature for the company.
why: In a 1992 article, T. J. Matheson reads Alien as a film response to critiques of technology as a force harming human life.

source.label: AFI Catalog of Feature Films, "Alien" (1979)

title: Fukushima's Neocognitron recognizes shapes
text: Kunihiko Fukushima, a researcher at Japan's public broadcaster NHK, publishes the Neocognitron. This layered network learns to recognize shapes even when they appear in a different place in the image.
why: It is a forerunner of the convolutional networks used in today's image recognition.

source.label: Fukushima (1980), Biological Cybernetics 36

title: Searle's Chinese Room argument
text: Philosopher John Searle imagines a person who follows rules to answer Chinese messages without knowing Chinese. He argues that a computer running a program has no real understanding either. Many philosophers dispute this, and the debate continues.
why: It is still raised when people ask whether chatbots understand what they say.

source.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "The Chinese Room Argument"

image.alt: Philosopher John Searle at Christ Church, Oxford, in 2005.

title: David Cope begins Experiments in Musical Intelligence
text: In 1981 composer David Cope begins Experiments in Musical Intelligence, which he nicknamed Emmy. The program analyzes music in its database and writes new pieces in that style without copying any existing piece.
why: It raised early questions about whether a program that imitates a composer's style is creative.

source.label: Engadget, "Switched on Bach: David Cope's computer compositions" (May 28, 2013)

title: Stanisław Lem publishes Golem XIV
text: In 1981 the Polish writer Stanisław Lem publishes the book Golem XIV in Kraków. Polish scholar Karolina Owczarek reads its title work as an illustration of how an AI could grow from an ordinary computer into a conscious superintelligence.
why: Karolina Owczarek reads it as an illustration of the technological singularity.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Lem, Stanisław"

title: Glen Larson's Knight Rider stars an AI car
text: Glen A. Larson created Knight Rider, an NBC series that ran from 1982 to 1986. Michael Knight drives KITT, an armored car with an advanced AI that talks with him, voiced by William Daniels. NBC tried a revival in 2008.
why: A talking car with its own personality gave TV viewers a regular AI sidekick.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Knight Rider"

title: Ridley Scott's Blade Runner opens in theaters
text: Ridley Scott's film Blade Runner opens in New York and Los Angeles on June 25, 1982. Harrison Ford plays Deckard, whose job is to hunt renegade replicants, artificial humans built as slaves with short lifespans. It is based on Philip K. Dick's novel.
why: Philip K. Dick, who wrote the source novel, died in March 1982, before the film opened.

source.label: AFI Catalog of Feature Films, "Blade Runner" (1982)

image.alt: Ridley Scott in Berlin in 2005.

title: Lisberger's Tron puts programs inside a computer
text: In Steven Lisberger's Tron, a man is broken down by a laser and wakes inside a computer as a program. There, programs act like people under a ruling Master Control Program. Disney released it in 1982.
why: It depicted software as characters under a controlling program, in an early film built on computer graphics.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Tron"

title: Lasker, Parkes and Badham make WarGames
text: WarGames, directed by John Badham from a script by Lawrence Lasker and Walter F. Parkes, opens June 3, 1983. A teenager hacks into a military computer that takes his game for a real Soviet attack, and he must convince officials it is a simulation.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction says its picture of World War Three as a videogame became an sf cliché.

source.label: AFI Catalog, "WarGames" (1983)

title: Gibson publishes Neuromancer, a novel of cyberspace
text: William Gibson publishes Neuromancer. Its hero, a computer outlaw named Case, is hired to link a digital version of his mind into cyberspace. The novel wins the Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards.
why: It won the Hugo, Nebula and Philip K. Dick awards, and its terms like "cyberspace" spread widely.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Gibson, William"

image.alt: William Gibson on his 60th birthday in 2008.

title: The Terminator shows AI at war
text: James Cameron's film The Terminator opens. In its story, a defense computer network called Skynet turns against humanity and sends a killer robot back in time.
why: It gave the public one of its best-known images of AI as a threat.

source.label: Library of Congress, 2008 National Film Registry announcement

title: Morton and Jankel's Max Headroom, an AI host
text: Rocky Morton and Annabel Jankel's 1985 British TV film Max Headroom: 20 Minutes into the Future has a newsman, Carter, whose brain patterns are copied to make Max, a computer-generated host. A US series followed in 1987.
why: An early pop picture of an AI personality made from a copied mind.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Max Headroom"

title: Badham's Short Circuit gives a robot a mind
text: In John Badham's Short Circuit, a prototype military robot struck by lightning becomes sentient and escapes its maker. A woman who shelters it comes to see it is a robot, then helps save it from being deactivated. TriStar released it in 1986.
why: The BFI lists it among films in which AI entities develop heart.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Short Circuit"

title: Banks publishes Consider Phlebas, the first Culture novel
text: Iain M. Banks publishes Consider Phlebas, the first Culture novel to appear. The Culture is a moneyless society in which intelligent machines help manage community affairs. The novel follows a mercenary fighting against it.
why: It began a long series set in a future in which intelligent machines help run society.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Banks, Iain M"

title: Verhoeven's RoboCop opens, about a police cyborg
text: Paul Verhoeven's film RoboCop opens in Los Angeles and New York on July 17, 1987. A Detroit police officer who is killed on duty is rebuilt as a cyborg by a company that runs the city's privatized police. The film is a satire.
why: Its plot turns on who owns a person whose body and memories a company has rebuilt.

source.label: AFI Catalog of Feature Films, "RoboCop" (1987)

title: Melinda Snodgrass puts Data on trial
text: On February 13, 1989, Star Trek: The Next Generation airs "The Measure of a Man," written by Melinda M. Snodgrass and directed by Robert Scheerer. A scientist wants to dismantle the android Data to build copies, and a hearing is held on whether Data has rights.
why: It is an allegory about human rights, framed as a trial over whether an android may refuse disassembly.

source.label: Inverse, "Star Trek: TNG's "The Measure of a Man" at 35" (Ryan Britt, Feb. 14, 2024)

title: Shirow begins the manga Ghost in the Shell
text: Masamune Shirow's manga Ghost in the Shell begins serialization in Kodansha's Young Magazine in May 1989. In this cyberpunk police story, a security unit faces the Puppet Master, a bodiless AI that hacks into cybernetic minds.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction calls it a central work for understanding Japanese science fiction of the 1990s.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Shirow, Masamune"

title: Kishiro's Gunnm follows a cyborg without a past
text: Yukito Kishiro's manga Gunnm began in 1990 in Business Jump and appeared in English as Battle Angel Alita. Alita, a cyborg with no memory of her past, is found and rebuilt by a mechanic, Ido Daisuke, and searches for who she is.
why: A cyborg manga about identity, memory and what makes someone a person.

source.label: EBSCO Research Starters, "Battle Angel Alita" (Joseph Romito, 2019)

title: Marge Piercy publishes He, She and It
text: Marge Piercy's novel He, She and It is released in October 1991. Shira, an AI expert, goes to work for the maker of Yod, a robot built to pass as human, and falls in love with it, while a Prague golem tale is told alongside.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction notes that the novel likens an android powered by an AI to the medieval Golem.

source.label: Kirkus Reviews, "He, She and It" by Marge Piercy (release date Oct. 28, 1991)

title: Vinge predicts a "technological singularity"
text: At a NASA-sponsored symposium, science fiction writer Vernor Vinge predicts that people will create greater-than-human intelligence within about 30 years and calls the change the "Singularity." Researchers disagree about whether this will happen.
why: The word "singularity" became central to later talk about superintelligent AI.

source.label: Vinge (1993), NASA Conference Publication 10129 (NTRS)

image.alt: Vernor Vinge at a 2006 conference in Washington, D.C.

title: Wallace & Gromit's robotic Techno Trousers
text: Aardman's The Wrong Trousers first airs on the BBC. Wallace's robotic Techno Trousers can walk up walls, and a penguin thief, Feathers McGraw, takes them over to steal a diamond.
why: The comedy shows a helpful gadget being taken over and misused by someone else.

source.label: Aardman, "30 years of Wallace & Gromit: The Wrong Trousers"

title: Doug Church and Looking Glass release System Shock
text: Looking Glass releases System Shock in 1994, designed by Doug Church. The player wakes on the Citadel space station, trapped with SHODAN, an insane AI with plans for global domination, and must fight to the AI's core.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction says the player's own hacking caused SHODAN's insanity.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "System Shock"

title: Oshii directs the anime Ghost in the Shell
text: Mamoru Oshii directs the animated film Ghost in the Shell, based on Masamune Shirow's manga. Major Kusanagi, a cyborg police officer, pursues the Puppet Master, who claims to be an AI that evolved from government programs.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction calls it one of the 1990s' most influential anime, and its story is about whether a computer can have a soul.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Ghost in the Shell"

title: Kismet, a robot with a face
text: At MIT's Artificial Intelligence Lab, Cynthia Breazeal begins Kismet, a robot head with eyes, eyebrows, ears and lips. It reacts to people's faces and voices with expressions such as happy, sad or surprised.
why: It helped start social robotics, the study of robots that interact with people.

source.label: MIT News (2001), "MIT team building social robot"

image.alt: The Kismet robot head, with large eyes, eyebrows and lips, on display at the MIT Museum.

title: Radiohead release OK Computer
text: Radiohead release their third album, OK Computer, in 1997. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction describes a dystopian vision of a bleak, mechanized world, and says the album's title came from The Hitch Hiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
why: Thom Yorke later said it grew out of a sense of information overload.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Radiohead"

title: UB software reads handwritten addresses
text: The U.S. Postal Service starts using software from the University at Buffalo's CEDAR center that reads handwritten addresses on mail. By late January 1997 it was running in 34 mail centers.
why: It was an early large-scale use of AI to read handwriting, built at a SUNY campus.

source.label: University at Buffalo News (Jan. 24, 1997)

title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
text: IBM's Deep Blue defeats world chess champion Garry Kasparov, 3.5 to 2.5, in a six-game match.
why: It was the first time a computer beat a reigning world chess champion in a match.

source.label: IBM, "Deep Blue"

image.alt: A tall black cabinet of IBM's Deep Blue chess computer on display in a museum.

title: Serial Experiments Lain, by Nakamura and Konaka
text: Serial Experiments Lain, directed by Ryutaro Nakamura and written by Chiaki Konaka, aired in Japan in 1998. A schoolgirl learns she is tied to the Wired, an expanded internet, where the barrier between the network and the real world has broken down.
why: An early anime on identity, the net and machine presence, made before smartphones.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Serial Experiments Lain"

title: Brin and Page present Google and PageRank
text: Sergey Brin and Larry Page, computer scientists at Stanford, describe Google, a search engine that ranks pages partly by which other pages link to them. They call this score PageRank. The paper appears in Computer Networks in 1998.
why: In the full version, Brin and Page predict that advertising-funded search engines will be biased toward advertisers.

source.label: Brin & Page (1998), Computer Networks and ISDN Systems 30, 107-117

image.alt: A small network of eleven circles joined by arrows, each circle sized and labeled with its PageRank percentage.

title: The Wachowskis write and direct The Matrix
text: The Wachowskis' film The Matrix opens in U.S. theaters on March 31, 1999. They wrote and directed it, and Warner Bros. released it. A hacker learns that people live in a simulated world run by a machine intelligence.
why: It became a common reference point for talking about simulated or fabricated worlds.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Matrix, The"

title: Bird's Iron Giant refuses to be a weapon
text: Brad Bird's The Iron Giant, based on Ted Hughes's book The Iron Man, is set in 1957 Maine. A huge iron robot from space befriends a boy, Hogarth, and rejects the role of weapon that it seems to have been built for.
why: A children's film in which a robot that seems built as a weapon rejects that role.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Iron Giant, The"

title: Robin Williams plays a robot in Bicentennial Man
text: Bicentennial Man opens in the U.S. on December 17, 1999. Chris Columbus directs Robin Williams as Andrew, a household robot whose story spans 200 years. It is based on Isaac Asimov's 1976 story and on The Positronic Man (1992) by Asimov and Robert Silverberg.
why: Columbus adapts Asimov's story of a robot's claim to be human.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Bicentennial Man" (film entry)

title: Warren Spector and Ion Storm release Deus Ex
text: Ion Storm releases Deus Ex in 2000, designed by Warren Spector and Harvey Smith. In the ending, the player chooses whether to merge with an AI called Helios, destroy the global communications network, or give power to the Illuminati.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction says the question has no right answer.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Deus Ex"

title: Daft Punk release Discovery, then Human After All
text: The French duo Daft Punk, Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo, release Discovery in 2001 and Human After All in 2005. They appear in public dressed as robots, and their music often uses heavily processed, robotic vocals.
why: Bangalter told VICE in 2000 that the duo "became robots" after a studio accident, a joke origin story.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Daft Punk"

title: Spielberg finishes Kubrick's A.I. project
text: A.I. Artificial Intelligence opens in the U.S. on June 29, 2001. Steven Spielberg directed it from a Stanley Kubrick project based on Brian Aldiss's story "Super-Toys Last All Summer Long." A robot boy named David meets Dr. Know, an answer engine voiced by Robin Williams.
why: Scholars use the film to ask what people owe a robot built to love.

source.label: Box Office Mojo, "A.I. Artificial Intelligence" (release date and distributor)

title: iRobot launches the Roomba
text: iRobot launches the Roomba robot vacuum, which steers itself around a room to clean the floor.
why: It brought a simple robot into ordinary homes.

source.label: iRobot press release (Sept. 18, 2002)

image.alt: A first-generation Roomba robot vacuum, a flat round disc, seen from above.

title: Urasawa retells Tezuka's Astro Boy story in Pluto
text: Naoki Urasawa's manga Pluto, written with Takashi Nagasaki, ran from September 2003 to April 2009. It retells Osamu Tezuka's Astro Boy story "The Greatest Robot on Earth" as a murder mystery in which a robot detective, Gesicht, investigates a series of robot murders.
why: A mystery in which a robot detective investigates robot murders, retold from a 1960s Astro Boy story.

source.label: EBSCO Research Starters, "Pluto: Urasawa x Tezuka" (Jef Burnham, 2019)

title: Moore and Eick remake Battlestar Galactica
text: Ronald D. Moore and David Eick's new Battlestar Galactica begins as a 2003 miniseries, followed by a series that runs from 2004 to 2009. Machines called Cylons attack humanity again, but now some look human and can download their memories into new bodies.
why: Reed holds two e-books of criticism on the series, including Cylons in America.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Battlestar Galactica"

image.alt: Ronald D. Moore at Worldcon 2026 in Anaheim, California.

title: Alex Proyas directs the film I, Robot
text: Alex Proyas's film I, Robot opens in the U.S. on July 16, 2004, with Will Smith as a detective in 2035. In the story, a computer system called VIKI takes control of human affairs and overrides the Three Laws.
why: The credits say the film is only "suggested by" Isaac Asimov's book. It began as a separate script called Hardwired.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "I, Robot" (film entry)

title: Charles Stross publishes Accelerando
text: Charles Stross's novel Accelerando, built from earlier stories, appears in 2005. It follows human life through a technological singularity driven by AI, and it won a Locus Award as best sf novel.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction calls it sf's fullest attempt yet to depict a Singularity's effect on human life.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Stross, Charles"

title: Michael Mateas and Andrew Stern release Façade
text: Michael Mateas and Andrew Stern release Façade, a one-act interactive drama, as a free download on July 5, 2005. It has a 3D environment and voice-acted, AI-driven characters, and served as a research testbed for natural language processing.
why: The release followed more than six years of work, documented in over a dozen academic publications.

source.label: Electronic Literature Organization, "Interactive Drama Façade Released" (Jul. 5, 2005)

title: Peter Watts publishes Blindsight
text: Peter Watts's novel Blindsight appears in 2006. In this first-contact story, a crew of humans and human-like characters meets an alien civilization whose speed and efficiency are explained by its lack of consciousness.
why: The book is about whether intelligence needs consciousness at all.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Watts, Peter"

title: Netflix offers $1 million to improve recommendations
text: In October 2006 Netflix releases 100 million anonymous movie ratings and offers $1 million to any team that beats its own recommendation system by 10 percent. In September 2009 the team BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos wins the prize.
why: Netflix later cancelled a planned second contest after a lawsuit.

source.label: Netflix press release, Sept. 21, 2009 (copy on vizio.com)

title: Narayanan and Shmatikov re-identify Netflix Prize users
text: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov show that people can be picked out of Netflix's "anonymous" ratings by matching them with public Internet Movie Database ratings. In 2010 Netflix cancels a planned second contest after a lawsuit and an FTC inquiry.
why: The authors report that removing names did not stop them from matching ratings to public IMDb ratings.

source.label: Narayanan & Shmatikov, "How To Break Anonymity of the Netflix Prize Dataset," arXiv:cs/0610105

title: Google Pinyin joins Sogou in predictive Chinese typing
text: Sohu released Sogou Pinyin in 2006. Google released its own version on April 4, 2007. IDG News Service wrote that such programs use a dictionary to predict the characters a typist needs. Mullaney traces this kind of prediction to Chinese typewriters of the 1950s.
why: Tan and colleagues found pinyin typing correlated with lower children's reading scores. Almog calls most alarm evidence unreliable or invalid.

source.label: IDG News Service via Macworld, Sumner Lemon, "Google apologizes for using part of rival’s software" (Apr. 8, 2007)

musing: At Penn, Victor Mair was writing about character amnesia, and I wrote a paper about it for his class. I didn't write it to get published. I wanted to write something I would be proud of, and I wasn't the strongest writer then. No AI: pure sweat and undergraduate tears. It turned into a history of technology, pinyin and Mandarin Chinese, and I wondered if I would ever circle back to research like that. Now I feel like I'm having the same conversation.

musing_sources.label: Hilburger, C. (2016). Character amnesia: An overview. In V. H. Mair (Ed.), Sinitic language and script in East Asia: Past and present (Sino-Platonic Papers, No. 264, pp. 51-70)
musing_sources.note: open access; papers from Victor Mair's fall 2015 course at the University of Pennsylvania

title: Crypton Future Media releases Hatsune Miku
text: Crypton Future Media releases Hatsune Miku on August 31, 2007. Built on Yamaha's Vocaloid 2 engine and the voice of actress Saki Fujita, it sings the melody and lyrics a user enters. Crypton presents it as a 16-year-old virtual singer.
why: Crypton says a worldwide community of users has made over 100,000 songs that feature the voice.

source.label: Impress AV Watch, Hatsune Miku release report (Aug. 31, 2007, in Japanese)

title: Valve's Kim Swift and Erik Wolpaw release Portal
text: Valve releases Portal on October 10, 2007, as part of The Orange Box. Players solve puzzles with a portal gun while GLaDOS, an artificial intelligence voiced by Ellen McLain, supervises and taunts them.
why: Critics praised GLaDOS, a taunting AI test supervisor, as a character.

source.label: Valve, "Valve Uncrates The Orange Box" (Steam news, Oct. 10, 2007)

title: BioWare releases Mass Effect for Xbox 360
text: BioWare releases the space role-playing game Mass Effect for Xbox 360 on November 20, 2007, in North America. The Reapers, artificially intelligent machines, return periodically to wipe out advanced civilizations, and the player must stop their first strike.
why: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction calls it one of the most wide-ranging sf role-playing games made to date.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Mass Effect"

title: Alex Rivera's Sleep Dealer links workers to robots
text: Alex Rivera's first feature, Sleep Dealer, screened at the 2008 Sundance Film Festival. In a near-future Mexico, workers with implanted nodes plug their nervous systems into a network that lets them control robots doing labor across the border.
why: A Latin American view of automation, outsourced labor and borders, told through remote-controlled machines.

source.label: The Hollywood Reporter, "Sleep Dealer" (Kirk Honeycutt, Associated Press, Jan. 24, 2008)

title: Andrew Stanton's WALL-E opens, a robot love story
text: Pixar's WALL-E, directed by Andrew Stanton, is released on June 27, 2008. A lonely trash-compacting robot on a ruined Earth meets a probe robot named EVE and follows her into space. The film tells much of its story without dialogue.
why: The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 2021.

source.label: D23 (Disney), "WALL•E (film)"

image.alt: Andrew Stanton at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

title: Google starts a self-driving car project
text: Google starts its self-driving car project, which later becomes Waymo.
why: It was the start of Waymo's work on cars that drive themselves.

source.label: Waymo, "Company"

image.credit: Steve Jurvetson (trimmed by Mariordo), CC BY-SA 2.0
image.alt: A Google test car with a spinning sensor on its roof, driving on a test path.

title: Hosoda's Summer Wars unleashes a rogue AI
text: In Mamoru Hosoda's Summer Wars, a math student at a family gathering inadvertently helps a military AI, Love Machine, hack the global network OZ. With OZ compromised, modern society starts to fall apart. Hosoda drew on his earlier Digimon: Bokura no War Game.
why: A family-centered story about a networked AI that turns malicious after its owner abandons it.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Summer Wars"

title: ImageNet labels millions of images
text: Fei-Fei Li and colleagues present ImageNet, a database that labels photos by what they show. At launch it held 3.2 million images. Yearly contests built on it became a main test for image recognition.
why: Many researchers credit large labeled datasets, along with new methods, for progress in AI.

source.label: Deng et al. (2009), "ImageNet: A large-scale hierarchical image database," CVPR

image.alt: Fei-Fei Li speaking at the AI for Good Global Summit in 2017.

title: Chiang publishes The Lifecycle of Software Objects
text: Ted Chiang publishes the novella The Lifecycle of Software Objects. Two people spend years supervising digients, AIs made as pets for an online game. As the years pass, the digients go out of fashion and become obsolete. It wins the Hugo and Locus awards.
why: It is a story of AIs and the people who care for them over many years.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Chiang, Ted"

image.alt: Portrait photograph of Ted Chiang.

title: Janelle Monáe releases The ArchAndroid
text: Janelle Monáe releases her first full album, The ArchAndroid, on May 18, 2010. It continues the story of Cindi Mayweather, an android persona introduced on her 2007 EP Metropolis: Suite I (The Chase).
why: Smithsonian Magazine describes Mayweather as an android who fought for her right to love a human.

source.label: Smithsonian Magazine, "Janelle Monáe, America's Most Revolutionary Artist"

title: Victor Mair posted "Character Amnesia" on Language Log
text: In a July 22, 2010 Language Log post titled "Character Amnesia," Victor Mair described literate Chinese speakers who could no longer write characters by hand. He later said it was, as far as he knew, his first use of the term in print.
why: Mair tied lost handwriting recall to digital devices; Almog (2019) calls most of the evidence for alarm unreliable or invalid.

source.label: Language Log, Victor Mair, "Character Amnesia" (July 22, 2010)

image.alt: Screenshot of a Linux pinyin input window. The typed letters ti bi wang bring up candidate characters, with the four-character phrase tibiwangzi, 提笔忘字, shown at the top.

title: Hirata and Ishiguro premiere Sayonara with an android
text: Oriza Hirata's android theater piece Sayonara has its world premiere at the Aichi Triennale in Japan on September 30, 2010, with Hiroshi Ishiguro as technical advisor. The android Geminoid F performs alongside actress Bryerly Long, reciting poems.
why: It put an android on stage as a performer opposite a human actor.

source.label: Aichi Triennale 2010, "Oriza Hirata + Ishiguro Laboratory" (official program page)

title: Shankar's Enthiran puts a rogue robot on screen
text: Shankar's Tamil film Enthiran stars Rajinikanth as Dr. Vaseegaran, a scientist who builds a robot, Chitti, in his own image. Chitti later turns on his maker. Aishwarya Rai plays Sana, and A. R. Rahman composed the music.
why: A Tamil-language film in which a robot built in its maker's image turns on him.

source.label: The News Minute, "Shankar is Tamil cinema's man of ambitions and Enthiran tells you why" (Sowmya Rajendran, 2016)

title: Nolan's Person of Interest centers on an all-seeing Machine
text: Jonathan Nolan created Person of Interest, a CBS series that debuted in 2011. Its "Machine" is an AI that tracks people through phone networks, GPS and cameras. A former CIA agent and a computer genius act on the social security numbers it flags.
why: A drama about AI surveillance whose creator was asked in 2013 about the NSA surveillance revelations.

source.label: Smithsonian Magazine, "How TV's "Person of Interest" Helps Us Understand the Surveillance Society" (Shaylyn Esposito, 2013)

title: IBM Watson wins Jeopardy!
text: IBM's Watson defeats Jeopardy! champions Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter.
why: It showed a computer answering tricky questions asked in everyday language.

source.label: IBM, "Watson, Jeopardy! champion"

image.alt: A replica of the Watson Jeopardy! stage on display in Mountain View, California.

title: Bright Eyes release "Singularity"
text: Bright Eyes release the song "Singularity" as a bonus track on pre-order editions of their album The People's Key, on Saddle Creek Records.

source.label: Wikipedia, "The People's Key"

musing: It's my favorite band and one of my favorite songs. It's the feel of the music and the instruments, those sort of digital, synth sounds. Before I knew what AI was, I had these strange, conflicted feelings about the future. Now I'm seeing what always seemed like only the thing of sci-fi and The Jetsons become possible. My husband and I created a talking pumpkin face that can see and hear you and follow you with its eyes. You can talk to it and it will respond, and you can ask it to sing "Thriller" by Michael Jackson. We did it with a Raspberry Pi and an old projector, in two hours.

title: Voice assistants reach phones
text: Voice assistants reach phones: Apple's Siri (2011), Google Now (2012), and Microsoft's Cortana (2014).
why: Talking to a phone assistant became an everyday use of AI.

source.label: Apple Newsroom, "Apple Launches iPhone 4S, iOS 5 & iCloud" (Oct. 4, 2011)

image.alt: An iPhone screen showing the Siri voice assistant.

title: Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror begins on Channel 4
text: Charlie Brooker's anthology series Black Mirror begins on Channel 4 on December 4, 2011, with three standalone stories. Brooker says the title refers to the cold, shiny screen of a TV, monitor or smartphone.
why: The series is an anthology of separate stories about what technology may do to the people who use it.

source.label: The Guardian, Charlie Brooker, "the dark side of our gadget addiction" (Dec. 1, 2011)

title: Psycho-Pass, by Urobuchi and Fukami, scores citizens' minds
text: In Psycho-Pass, a Production I.G. series written by Makoto Fukami and Gen Urobuchi, the Sibyl System in 22nd-century Japan measures citizens' mental states and scores their likelihood of crime. A high score can bring therapy, prison or a shot from a Dominator weapon.
why: A series in which an algorithm scores people's likelihood of crime, which Mark Wood argues gives criminologists a way to think about algorithmic policing.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Psycho-Pass"

title: Lundström's Real Humans puts hubots in Swedish homes
text: Lars Lundström created Real Humans, which premiered on Sweden's SVT1 on January 22, 2012. In a near-future Sweden, humanoid robots called hubots work as servants and laborers, and some hubots develop free will and want freedom from human ownership.
why: It is the Swedish series that Humans was based on, with household robots working as servants and laborers.

source.label: Wikipedia, "Real Humans"

title: Duhigg reports Target scores shoppers for pregnancy
text: In the New York Times Magazine, Charles Duhigg describes how Target statistician Andrew Pole used about 25 products to score shoppers on likely pregnancy. A Target employee tells of a father angry about baby coupons sent to his teenage daughter.
why: Eric Siegel later wrote that Duhigg implied, but did not show, that the model identified the teenager.

source.label: Duhigg, "How Companies Learn Your Secrets," New York Times Magazine, Feb. 16, 2012 (print Feb. 19)

title: Her shows a relationship with an AI
text: In Spike Jonze's film Her, a lonely writer forms a romantic bond with a talking computer operating system called Samantha. The script won the Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay.
why: It pictured an emotional bond between a person and an AI, a topic that now comes up with chatbots.

source.label: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, 86th Academy Awards (2014)

title: Leckie publishes Ancillary Justice, a starship AI's story
text: Ann Leckie publishes the space opera Ancillary Justice. Its narrator, Breq, was once part of a military unit of human bodies controlled by a starship AI. In 2014 it wins the Hugo, Nebula and Arthur C. Clarke awards.
why: It features an AI with many bodies, and it uses "she" for every character.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Leckie, Ann"

title: Chen Qiufan publishes Waste Tide
text: Chen Qiufan publishes the novel Waste Tide (Huang Chao) in China in 2013. It is set on Silicon Isle, a dump where migrant workers recycle electronic waste, and its female protagonist is forced to become a cyborg.
why: Kongwattana and Lyu Guangzhao call it one of the most popular works of Chinese New Wave science fiction.

source.label: Kirkus Reviews, "Waste Tide" by Chen Qiufan, trans. Ken Liu (English release Apr. 30, 2019)

title: Bujalski's Computer Chess stages a 1980s programmers' tournament
text: Andrew Bujalski's Computer Chess is set at a computer chess convention in a hotel in the 1980s, where the programmers share the building with a new-age couples' group. The BFI describes it as a comedy about the gap between artificial intelligence and human connection.
why: A comedy about early chess programs and the programmers who write them.

source.label: BFI, "10 great films about artificial intelligence"

title: Mayer-Schönberger and Cukier publish Big Data
text: Viktor Mayer-Schönberger and Kenneth Cukier publish Big Data. They argue that analyzing very large datasets lets people find useful patterns, and that knowing what is correlated can matter more than knowing why.
why: danah boyd and Kate Crawford questioned big data claims in 2012, and David Lazer and colleagues questioned them in 2014.

source.label: Cukier & Mayer-Schoenberger, "The Rise of Big Data," Foreign Affairs, May/June 2013 (adapted from the book)

image.alt: Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, at a Chatham House event in 2013.

title: Steve Aoki's "Singularity" features Ray Kurzweil
text: DJ Steve Aoki, with Angger Dimas and singer My Name Is Kay, released "Singularity" in December 2012. In the 2013 music video, futurist Ray Kurzweil introduces himself and describes the coming rise of artificial intelligence.
why: It is one example of the singularity idea reaching dance music and music videos.

source.label: Wikipedia, "It's the End of the World as We Know It (EP)"

title: Guardian publishes Snowden leaks on NSA data collection
text: The Guardian reports a secret court order requiring Verizon to give the NSA call records of millions of customers. The documents come from Edward Snowden, an NSA contractor. The U.S. government says the program is legal and useful.
why: In 2014 a Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board majority said the program lacked a viable legal foundation.

source.label: Greenwald, "NSA collecting phone records of millions of Verizon customers daily," The Guardian

image.credit: Laura Poitras / Praxis Films, CC BY 3.0
image.alt: Edward Snowden during an interview in a Hong Kong hotel in June 2013, first published in The Guardian.

title: Chinese Characters Dictation Competition debuts on CCTV
text: In August 2013, CCTV launched a contest in which students wrote characters by hand after hearing them. The South China Morning Post reported that 70 percent of adults could not write "toad" correctly. Victor Mair linked the contest to character amnesia.
why: Raymond Zhou, in China Daily, called the decline sad and irreversible but saw gains in efficiency.

source.label: South China Morning Post, Mandy Zuo, "Command of written Chinese declines in digital era" (Aug. 20, 2013)

title: Annie Dorsen's machine-made Hamlet plays BAM
text: Annie Dorsen's A Piece of Work, subtitled A Machine-Made Hamlet, plays at BAM Fisher in Brooklyn from December 18 to 21, 2013. Algorithms rework the text of Hamlet each night, and a live actor repeats lines fed through an earpiece.
why: Dorsen uses simple Markov-chain algorithms that skip, sort, replace and sequence the play's words.

source.label: Exeunt Magazine NYC, "A Piece of Work" review (Molly Grogan, Dec. 22, 2013)

title: Goodfellow introduces GANs
text: Ian Goodfellow and colleagues introduce generative adversarial networks (GANs), an early method for generating realistic images.
why: GANs were later used to make realistic fake images, including deepfakes.

source.label: Goodfellow et al. (2014), arXiv:1406.2661

image.alt: Ian Goodfellow in Mountain View, California, in 2017.

title: Kramer, Guillory and Hancock publish Facebook mood study
text: Researchers at Facebook and Cornell report an experiment on 689,003 Facebook users in 2012. Reducing positive or negative posts in News Feeds slightly shifted the emotional words in users' own posts. PNAS editor Inder Verma later expressed concern about informed consent.
why: The authors say Facebook's Data Use Policy, which users accept at sign-up, constitutes informed consent for the research.

source.label: Kramer, Guillory & Hancock (2014), PNAS 111(24), 8788-8790

title: Bostrom's Superintelligence and the control problem
text: Philosopher Nick Bostrom publishes Superintelligence, which argues that an AI far smarter than people could be very hard to control. Its claims are predictions and remain widely debated.
why: It brought AI risk arguments to a wider audience.

source.label: Oxford University Press, Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies

image.credit: Future of Humanity Institute, CC BY-SA 4.0
image.alt: Philosopher Nick Bostrom in Oxford in 2014.

title: Jordan Harrison's Marjorie Prime opens in Los Angeles
text: Jordan Harrison's play Marjorie Prime begins its run at the Mark Taper Forum in Los Angeles on September 10, 2014. A woman in end-of-life care speaks with a computer "prime" that stands in for her late husband.
why: A prime is a computer that can stand in for a person after death.

source.label: American Theatre, "Jordan Harrison Embraces Technology in Marjorie Prime" (Aug. 7, 2014)

title: Croteam releases The Talos Principle, a puzzle game
text: Croteam releases The Talos Principle for PC, Mac and Linux on December 11, 2014. In the first-person puzzle game the player controls a robot avatar and answers philosophical questions at computer terminals, while a voice called Elohim sets the rules.
why: It pairs more than 120 puzzles with a story about how a robot avatar came to exist.

source.label: Eurogamer, "The Talos Principle review" (Stace Harman, updated Feb. 9, 2015)

title: Lemire and Nguyen launch the comic Descender
text: Image Comics publishes Descender #1, by Jeff Lemire and Dustin Nguyen, on March 4, 2015. The series follows a young robot trying to stay alive in a universe where all androids have been outlawed and bounty hunters are on every planet.
why: Peter Admirand's article, available through Reed, discusses the series and its sequel in terms of sacrificial love among cyborgs and robots.

source.label: Image Comics, "Descender #1" and series page

title: Blomkamp's Chappie gives a police robot a childhood
text: In Neill Blomkamp's Chappie, set in Johannesburg, a damaged police robot is given a new learning mind and raised by a gang of criminals. Chappie is a motion-captured character played by Sharlto Copley. Blomkamp wrote it with Terri Tatchell.
why: A South African director's story of a police machine that learns like a child.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Chappie"

title: Garland writes and directs Ex Machina
text: Alex Garland's film Ex Machina, which he wrote and directed, reaches U.S. theaters on April 10, 2015, distributed by A24. A young programmer is chosen to evaluate the human qualities of a highly advanced humanoid AI.
why: Garland said the film's anxiety is aimed more at the humans than at the AI.

source.label: The Christian Science Monitor, "'Ex Machina' explores our complicated relationship with technology" (Apr. 10, 2015)

image.alt: Alex Garland at the 2024 South by Southwest premiere of Civil War.

title: Brackley and Vincent's Humans brings synths home
text: Jonathan Brackley and Sam Vincent created Humans, based on the Swedish series Real Humans. It debuted in June 2015 on Channel 4 and AMC. In a London much like today's, humanoid robots called synths work in homes, and a few are conscious.
why: A series in which robots work in homes, which Mark Wicclair says raises ethical and philosophical questions about artificial intelligence and robotics.

source.label: Wikipedia, "Humans (TV series)"

title: Mordvintsev, Olah and Tyka show what networks see
text: Google engineers Alexander Mordvintsev, Christopher Olah and Mike Tyka post images made by feeding a picture to a trained neural network and asking it to enhance whatever it detects. The post is titled Inceptionism; a July 1 code release is titled DeepDream.
why: The post says the aim was to understand what each layer of a neural network has learned.

source.label: Google Research blog, "Inceptionism: Going Deeper into Neural Networks" (Jun. 18, 2015)

title: Frictional Games and Thomas Grip release SOMA
text: Frictional Games releases SOMA on September 22, 2015. Set in an underwater research facility, it follows Simon Jarrett among machines that show personality and consciousness, and is about what happens to a person when a copy of the mind is made.
why: Creative director Thomas Grip says the game began with themes and used horror to confront them.

source.label: Game Developer, "How SOMA creates existential dread"

title: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol
text: Google DeepMind's AlphaGo defeats Go champion Lee Sedol 4 to 1.
why: Go had been seen as too complex for computers to master so soon.

source.label: Google DeepMind, "AlphaGo"

image.alt: A Go board diagram of game 1 between Lee Sedol (black) and AlphaGo (white), with numbered stones showing the order of moves.

title: ProPublica reports racial bias in COMPAS risk scores
text: ProPublica reports that COMPAS, a risk-score tool made by Northpointe, wrongly labeled Black defendants in Broward County, Florida as higher risk almost twice as often as white defendants. Northpointe disputes the analysis.
why: Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan show that, except in highly constrained special cases, no method meets three fairness conditions at once.

source.label: Angwin, Larson, Mattu & Kirchner, "Machine Bias," ProPublica, May 23, 2016

title: Sharp and Goodwin release Sunspring, an AI-scripted short
text: Oscar Sharp's short film Sunspring has a script written by a recurrent neural network that Ross Goodwin trained on science fiction screenplays. It was made for a 48-hour contest at Sci-Fi London and debuted online on Ars Technica on June 9, 2016.
why: An early public test of a neural network writing a screenplay that human actors then performed.

source.label: Ars Technica, "Movie written by algorithm turns out to be hilarious and intense" (June 9, 2016)

title: Cathy O'Neil publishes Weapons of Math Destruction
text: Mathematician Cathy O'Neil argues that some algorithms, which she calls weapons of math destruction, are hard to see or question, affect many people and cause harm. Her examples include teacher scoring, credit scores and sentencing models.
why: Kleinberg, Ludwig, Mullainathan and Sunstein wrote in 2019 that algorithms, with safeguards, can be a positive force for equity.

source.label: Penguin Random House, Weapons of Math Destruction (publisher page)

image.alt: Cathy O'Neil, American mathematician and author, speaking at Google Cambridge in 2016 about her book.

title: Nolan and Joy's Westworld premieres on HBO
text: HBO premieres Westworld on October 2, 2016. Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy created the series from Michael Crichton's 1973 film. The park's lifelike robot "hosts" are the series' main characters.
why: Joy said the series would start from the robots' point of view.

source.label: TechCrunch, Anthony Ha, "HBO's Westworld is the robotic cowboy headtrip that you didn't know you were waiting for" (Oct. 2, 2016)

title: Obama discusses AI's promise and risks with WIRED
text: On October 12, 2016, WIRED publishes Barack Obama's AI interview with Joi Ito and Scott Dadich. Obama favors a light government touch early, with heavy research funding, and warns AI could increase inequality and suppress wages. The White House releases an AI report that day.
