why: A sitting president framed AI as a policy question about jobs, fairness and the role of government.

source.label: WIRED, "Barack Obama, Neural Nets, Self-Driving Cars, and the Future of the World" (Oct. 12, 2016)

image.credit: Official White House Photo by Pete Souza, public domain
image.alt: Official portrait of President Barack Obama in the Oval Office, December 2012.

title: Yoko Taro and PlatinumGames release NieR: Automata
text: NieR:Automata, directed by Yoko Taro and developed by PlatinumGames for Square Enix, reaches North America on March 7, 2017. The action role-playing game follows YoRHa, a force of android soldiers, in a war against machine lifeforms.
why: One scholarly article argues that the androids and machines perform human values such as beauty, love and consumerism.

source.label: PlatinumGames, "NieR:Automata"

title: The transformer and large language models
text: Google researchers introduce the transformer (2017); OpenAI's GPT (2018) and Google's BERT (2018) show what large pretrained language models can do.
why: Most of today's large language models are built on the transformer design.

source.label: Vaswani et al. (2017), arXiv:1706.03762

image.alt: A diagram of the transformer model, with stacked encoder and decoder blocks and attention layers.

title: Villeneuve's Blade Runner 2049 returns to the replicants
text: Denis Villeneuve's Blade Runner 2049 continues the replicant story. K, a replicant blade runner played by Ryan Gosling, follows a memory to the truth about his own identity, while the Wallace Corporation builds a new generation of obedient replicants.
why: It continues the first film's replicant story and ties K's identity to a memory and to his relationship with the hologram Joi.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Blade Runner 2049"

title: Hanson Robotics' Sophia is granted Saudi citizenship
text: At the Future Investment Initiative conference in Riyadh on October 25, 2017, Saudi Arabia announces citizenship for Sophia, a humanoid robot made by Hanson Robotics. Dezeen reports it was unclear whether she would have the same rights as human citizens.
why: Parviainen and Coeckelbergh argue that Sophia's appearances helped the social robot market.

source.label: Dezeen, "Saudi Arabia becomes first country to grant citizenship to a robot" (Alice Morby, Oct. 26, 2017)

title: Gender Shades finds bias in face analysis
text: Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru test three commercial face-analysis systems. The systems misclassified gender for darker-skinned women up to 34.7% of the time, and for lighter-skinned men at most 0.8%.
why: It is widely cited as an early push to test AI for unequal error rates across groups.

source.label: Buolamwini & Gebru (2018), "Gender Shades," PMLR 81

image.alt: Joy Buolamwini speaking at Wikimania 2018 in Cape Town, South Africa.

title: Safiya Noble publishes Algorithms of Oppression
text: Safiya Umoja Noble argues that search engines are not neutral. She shows that Google results for terms like "black girls" returned pornographic content, and she links this to advertising and to the market power of a few companies.
why: Noble argues that search ranking can reflect and spread social bias.

source.label: NYU Press, Algorithms of Oppression (publisher page)

image.alt: Safiya Umoja Noble speaking at the re:publica conference in Berlin, May 2018.

title: Observer reveals Cambridge Analytica's use of Facebook data
text: The Observer reports that Cambridge Analytica obtained data on more than 50 million Facebook profiles. Facebook says the app developer gained access legitimately but broke its rules by passing the data on, and says it was not a data breach.
why: Margaret Hu notes a record $5 billion Federal Trade Commission penalty against Facebook in 2019.

source.label: Cadwalladr & Graham-Harrison, "Revealed: 50 million Facebook profiles harvested for Cambridge Analytica," The Guardian/Observer

title: Quantic Dream releases Detroit: Become Human
text: Quantic Dream, whose director is David Cage, releases Detroit: Become Human for PlayStation 4 on May 25, 2018. Players switch between three androids in a near-future Detroit, and their choices shape the story.
why: A scholar reads it as a political text, and the player makes its narrative choices.

source.label: PlayStation.Blog, "Detroit: Become Human, David Cage on Creating the Perfect Android" (June 22, 2017); release date from OpenCritic

title: EU General Data Protection Regulation takes effect
text: The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation begins to apply. It gives people rights over their personal data and limits decisions made only by automated processing, such as profiling. Scholars disagree about how much explanation of such decisions people can demand.
why: Companies serving European customers had to follow it; Frey and Presidente report lower profits for technology firms, mainly smaller ones.

source.label: GDPR Article 99, "Entry into force and application" (unofficial copy at gdpr-info.eu)

title: Reuters reports Amazon dropped a biased hiring tool
text: Reuters, citing five people familiar with the effort, reports that Amazon built an experimental tool to score job applicants' résumés. The system learned from ten years of mostly male résumés and penalized the word "women's." Amazon says recruiters never used it to evaluate candidates.
why: Reuters reports that a model trained on past hiring repeated past bias.

source.label: Dastin, "Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women," Reuters, Oct. 10, 2018

title: Christie's sells an AI-made portrait
text: Christie's in New York sells Portrait of Edmond de Belamy, a print made with a GAN by the French group Obvious, for more than $430,000. Critics noted that the group used code written by another artist, Robbie Barrat.
why: The sale prompted public debate over who counts as the artist when AI is used.

source.label: MIT Technology Review (Oct. 26, 2018)

title: Masakhane builds tools for African languages
text: Masakhane, a grassroots research community, forms to build translation and language tools for African languages, by and for Africans. The name means "we build together" in isiZulu.
why: It is a community effort to build language tools for African languages, which have had few resources.

source.label: Orife et al. (2020), "Masakhane: Machine Translation for Africa"

title: Frant Gwo's The Wandering Earth adapts Liu Cixin
text: Frant Gwo's The Wandering Earth, based on a Liu Cixin novella, is set in a future where engines built across the planet move Earth away from an aging Sun. The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction notes machines and malfunctioning AIs in the year 2061.
why: A Chinese science fiction film in which machine systems and AIs malfunction in 2061.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Wandering Earth, The"

title: Miller's Love, Death and Robots collects animated shorts
text: Love, Death + Robots, created by Tim Miller for Netflix, is an animated anthology, mostly adapting short stories, with each episode made by a different studio. Season one included stories by John Scalzi, Alastair Reynolds and Ken Liu.
why: Short animated stories brought robots and AI to a streaming audience in many animation styles.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Love, Death and Robots"

title: Shoshana Zuboff publishes The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
text: Shoshana Zuboff argues that some technology companies collect data about human behavior, turn it into predictions and sell those predictions to others. She calls this surveillance capitalism and says it undermines democracy.
why: Evgeny Morozov wrote in 2019 that Zuboff does not weigh rival frameworks.

source.label: PublicAffairs, The Age of Surveillance Capitalism (publisher page)

image.credit: Alexander von Humboldt Institut for internet and society, CC BY 3.0
image.alt: Shoshana Zuboff speaking at the Alexander von Humboldt Institute for Internet and Society in Berlin, November 2019.

title: Mario Klingemann's AI portraits go to Sotheby's
text: Sotheby's offers Mario Klingemann's Memories of Passersby I in London on March 6, 2019, calling it the first self-contained, generative work of AI on the market. Two screens show endlessly changing portraits of faces that do not exist. The estimate was 30,000 to 40,000 pounds.
why: A major auction house treated a running neural network as a work of art for sale.

source.label: Reuters via The Jakarta Post, "AI portrait joins Warhol, Basquiat and Freud at London auction" (Mar. 2, 2019)

title: Ian McEwan publishes Machines Like Me
text: Ian McEwan's novel Machines Like Me is released in April 2019. In a 1982 where Alan Turing is still alive, a man buys an android named Adam, and a love triangle forms with the woman living upstairs.
why: A literary novelist uses an android to test ideas about ethics, love and machine consciousness.

source.label: Kirkus Reviews, "Machines Like Me" by Ian McEwan (release date Apr. 23, 2019)

title: Holly Herndon releases Proto with her AI Spawn
text: Holly Herndon releases the album Proto on May 10, 2019, on 4AD. Her label says she made it with an ensemble of vocalists, developers and an AI she calls Spawn. Spawn first appeared in 2018 on "Godmother," with Jlin.
why: Her label lists an AI among the collaborators on the album.

source.label: The FADER, "Holly Herndon announces new album PROTO" (David Renshaw, Mar. 11, 2019)

title: Barbican opens AI: More than Human
text: The Barbican Centre in London opens AI: More Than Human on May 16, 2019. The exhibition mixes historical objects such as an Enigma machine with film and literature references and new installations by artists including Es Devlin and Lawrence Lek.
why: Barbican International Enterprises called AI a key marker of the zeitgeist and a stimulus for creativity.

source.label: Dezeen, "The Barbican dives deep into artificial intelligence with More Than Human exhibition" (Rima Sabina Aouf, May 16, 2019)

title: Ruha Benjamin publishes Race After Technology
text: Princeton professor Ruha Benjamin argues that new technologies can hide or deepen racial discrimination while seeming neutral. She calls this the "New Jim Code" and describes designs that amplify bias, ignore it while replicating it, or try to fix it and do the opposite.
why: Kleinberg, Ludwig, Mullainathan and Sunstein wrote in 2019 that algorithms can make discrimination easier to detect, given safeguards.

source.label: Reed catalog record, Race After Technology (Polity, 2019; publisher summary)

image.credit: Data & Society Research Institute, CC BY 3.0
image.alt: Princeton professor Ruha Benjamin presenting at the Data & Society Research Institute's Databites series in 2019.

title: Crawford and Paglen open Training Humans in Milan
text: Kate Crawford and Trevor Paglen's exhibition Training Humans opens at Fondazione Prada in Milan on September 12, 2019. It retraces the history of images used to train AI systems to see and categorize the world. Their essay Excavating AI accompanied it.
why: In the essay, Crawford and Paglen argue that labels in ImageNet's person category carry judgments about people.

source.label: Prada Group Journal, "Fondazione Prada: Training Humans" (2019)

title: Hugging Face opens up language models
text: Hugging Face describes Transformers, a free, open-source library for downloading and using pretrained language models. Its Hub became a main place to share open models and datasets, listing over 2 million models by 2026.
why: It gave students and researchers a free library for using pretrained language models.

source.label: Wolf et al. (2019), "HuggingFace's Transformers," arXiv:1910.03771

image.alt: Thomas Wolf, a co-founder of Hugging Face, speaking on stage at the Slush conference.

title: Nick Walton releases AI Dungeon 2 text game
text: Nick Walton, then a Brigham Young University student, releases AI Dungeon 2 as a Google Colab notebook on December 5, 2019. The text adventure uses OpenAI's GPT-2 language model to generate and narrate the story, and has 100,000 players within a week.
why: Hua and Raley study the game in a Digital Humanities Quarterly article on players' hobbyist relations with machine learning.

source.label: Hua and Raley, "Playing With Unicorns: AI Dungeon and Citizen NLP," Digital Humanities Quarterly 14(4), 2020

title: OpenAI announces GPT-3
text: OpenAI announces GPT-3, a large language model. ChatGPT, a chatbot built on OpenAI's models, follows in November 2022.
why: It showed a bigger model could do new tasks from a few examples in the prompt.

source.label: Brown et al. (2020), arXiv:2005.14165

title: Schrader's I'm Your Man gives a scholar a robot partner
text: In Maria Schrader's German film, the scholar Alma agrees to live with Tom, an android built to be her ideal partner. Schrader and Jan Schomburg wrote it from a story by Emma Braslavsky. Maren Eggert won Best Leading Performance at the Berlin festival.
why: Companion AI told as a romantic comedy about what an android partner does to a person.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "I'm Your Man"

title: Kogonada's After Yang follows a family's android loss
text: In Kogonada's After Yang, the family's android 'technosapien,' Yang, stops working. Jake and Kyra, played by Colin Farrell and Jodie Turner-Smith, face the loss, and so does their adopted daughter Mika, who had come to rely on Yang as her main caregiver.
why: A film about care for an android and grief when it stops working.

source.label: BFI, "10 great films about artificial intelligence"

title: DALL-E turns text into images
text: OpenAI announces DALL-E, a system that creates images from short text descriptions. In 2022, newer text-to-image tools became widely available to the public.
why: It raised new questions about art, copyright, and fake images.

source.label: OpenAI, "DALL-E: Creating images from text"

title: Bender and colleagues publish "Stochastic Parrots"
text: Emily Bender, Timnit Gebru, Angelina McMillan-Major and Margaret Mitchell publish "On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots," which argues that very large language models carry risks: environmental cost, biased training data, and fluent text with no grounding in meaning.
why: Its phrase "stochastic parrots" became shorthand in debates over whether chatbots understand language.

source.label: Bender et al. (2021), ACM FAccT

image.credit: Bender, Gebru, McMillan-Major and Shmitchell (ACM), CC BY 4.0
image.alt: The first page of the 2021 paper On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots, with the title, authors and abstract.

title: Kazuo Ishiguro publishes Klara and the Sun
text: Kazuo Ishiguro's novel Klara and the Sun is released in March 2021. Klara, an Artificial Friend sold as a companion to a sick teenager, tells of her devotion to the girl and her family.
why: In this novel, Ishiguro, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2017, writes an artificial companion story.

source.label: Kirkus Reviews, "Klara and the Sun" by Kazuo Ishiguro (release date Mar. 2, 2021)

title: AlphaFold predicts protein shapes
text: DeepMind publishes AlphaFold 2 in Nature, with open code, showing it can predict the 3D shape of proteins with high accuracy. A week later, a free database of predicted structures opened, starting with nearly every human protein.
why: Protein shapes guide drug and disease research; the work later won a Nobel Prize.

source.label: Jumper et al. (2021), Nature 596

image.credit: John Jumper et al., CC BY 4.0
image.alt: A figure from the AlphaFold paper comparing predicted protein structures with structures measured in experiments.

title: Kai-Fu Lee and Chen Qiufan publish AI 2041
text: Kai-Fu Lee and Chen Qiufan publish AI 2041: Ten Visions for Our Future in September 2021. Chen's ten stories, each paired with an essay by Lee, describe AI developments over the next 20 years, from deep learning to smart weapons.
why: It is a recent example of fiction used to explain near-term AI to general readers.

source.label: Locus, Gary K. Wolfe, "Reviews AI 2041: Ten Visions for Our Future" (Feb. 2, 2022)

title: UB forms an AI and data science institute
text: The University at Buffalo announces its Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Data Science on November 22, 2021. It combines two units founded in 2018, the Artificial Intelligence Institute and the Institute for Computational and Data Science. David Doermann becomes director.
why: It brought a SUNY campus's two AI and data science units under one institute.

source.label: UBNow, "UB forms Institute for Artificial Intelligence and Data Science" (Nov. 22, 2021)

image.alt: The interior entrance to Lockwood Memorial Library at the University at Buffalo. The institute is based in Lockwood.

title: BLOOM, an open multilingual language model
text: The BigScience project, coordinated by Hugging Face with more than 1,000 researchers from 70+ countries, releases BLOOM. The 176-billion-parameter model is free to download and covers 46 human languages, including Swahili, Yoruba and other African languages.
why: It showed a large language model could be built in the open by a broad research community.

source.label: Hugging Face, "Introducing The World's Largest Open Multilingual Language Model: BLOOM"

title: Jason Allen wins state fair with Midjourney image
text: At the 2022 Colorado State Fair, Jason Allen wins first place in digital arts with Théâtre D'opéra Spatial, made with the AI program Midjourney. He says he told officials how it was made. The win starts a public debate over what counts as art.
why: The judges said they would still have picked the piece, and a fair spokesperson called the dispute a broader conversation.

source.label: Smithsonian Magazine, "Art Made With Artificial Intelligence Wins at State Fair" (Sept. 6, 2022)

title: Refik Anadol's Unsupervised opens at MoMA
text: Refik Anadol's Unsupervised goes on view at the Museum of Modern Art on November 19, 2022. Three AI artworks interpret more than 200 years of art from MoMA's collection on a 24-by-24-foot wall, and respond to light, movement and weather in the lobby.
why: MoMA's curator, Michelle Kuo, said the work is visionary and explores dreams, hallucination and irrationality.

source.label: The Museum of Modern Art, press release "Refik Anadol: Unsupervised" (Nov. 1, 2022)

title: ChatGPT launches to the public
text: OpenAI releases ChatGPT, a free chatbot built on its language models. In October 2025, OpenAI's CEO said the company counts more than 800 million weekly users.
why: It brought generative AI into everyday use for many students, workers and teachers.

source.label: OpenAI, "Introducing ChatGPT" (Nov. 30, 2022)

image.credit: Screenshot of ChatGPT output, Public domain
image.alt: A 2023 screenshot in which ChatGPT writes a confident summary of a news article from a made-up web address.

title: The Dalles drops suit; Google water use disclosed
text: In December 2022, The Dalles, Oregon, settled its lawsuit against The Oregonian and released records of Google's data center water use. The city had called the figures a trade secret. The Oregonian then reported that Google's use nearly tripled in five years.
why: Google then said it would stop treating site-level water numbers as trade secrets at its U.S. data centers.

source.label: Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, "Oregon's city of The Dalles agrees to reveal Google's local water usage" (Dec. 15, 2022)

image.alt: Exterior of a Google data center building in The Dalles, Oregon.

title: New York City schools ban, then allow, ChatGPT
text: In January 2023, New York City's education department blocked ChatGPT on school devices and networks, citing worries about learning and accuracy. In May 2023, Chancellor David Banks reversed course. He said the ban came partly from "knee-jerk fear."
why: One large district's quick reversal shows how fast school AI policy changed after ChatGPT appeared.

source.label: Chalkbeat, David C. Banks, "ChatGPT caught NYC schools off guard. Now, we're determined to embrace its potential" (May 18, 2023)

title: NSF funds UB-led AI institute for children
text: The National Science Foundation announces a $20 million AI institute led by the University at Buffalo on January 9, 2023. It is meant to build tools that screen children's speech and language and support intervention. The Institute of Education Sciences also funds it.
why: It is a federally funded, SUNY-led AI project aimed at a shortage of speech-language pathologists.

source.label: National Science Foundation, "NSF announces new AI institute" (Jan. 9, 2023)

image.alt: Furnas Hall and Bell Hall on the North Campus of the University at Buffalo, Amherst, New York, July 2020.

title: Andersen, McKernan and Ortiz sue Stability AI
text: Artists Sarah Andersen, Kelly McKernan and Karla Ortiz file a class-action copyright suit in federal court in California on January 13, 2023, against Stability AI, Midjourney and DeviantArt. Their lawyers say image generators were built on artists' work without consent.
why: Courts were asked whether training image generators on artists' work infringes copyright.

source.label: CourtListener, docket for Andersen v. Stability AI Ltd., No. 3:23-cv-00201 (N.D. Cal.)

title: Researchers sign open letters on AI risk
text: The Future of Life Institute publishes an open letter urging a six-month pause on training AI systems more powerful than GPT-4. In May, many researchers sign a statement that AI extinction risk should be a global priority. Critics say these warnings distract from present harms.
why: It moved arguments about AI risk into mainstream news.

source.label: Future of Life Institute, "Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter"

title: Turnitin launches AI detector; Vanderbilt turns it off
text: On April 4, 2023, Turnitin switched on AI writing detection for educators. In August, Vanderbilt University disabled it, citing false positives and possible bias. A 2023 study found seven detectors misclassified over half of essays by non-native English writers as AI-written.
why: Schools adopted detectors to catch AI cheating, but false flags can harm honest students.

source.label: Vanderbilt University, "Guidance on AI Detection and Why We're Disabling Turnitin's AI Detector" (Aug. 16, 2023)

title: Ghostwriter977's AI Drake and Weeknd song is pulled
text: An anonymous TikTok user, Ghostwriter977, posts "Heart on My Sleeve," which uses AI-generated voices imitating Drake and The Weeknd. It is streamed hundreds of thousands of times before it is pulled on April 17, 2023. Universal Music Group objects.
why: It started a public dispute over voice rights and the use of artists' recordings to train AI.

source.label: The FADER, "Viral song with AI-generated Drake and The Weeknd vocals removed from streaming" (Apr. 18, 2023)

title: Geoffrey Hinton leaves Google to warn about AI
text: Geoffrey Hinton, whose neural network research helped lay the groundwork for today's chatbots, announces on May 1, 2023, that he has left Google. He tells the BBC some chatbot dangers are "quite scary" and that he left to speak freely. He calls Google "very responsible."
why: A deep learning pioneer warned about AI risks, and Meredith Whittaker said the focus distracts from current harms.

source.label: BBC News, "AI 'godfather' Geoffrey Hinton warns of dangers as he quits Google" (May 2, 2023)

image.alt: Geoffrey Hinton in 2026.

title: Sam Altman asks the Senate to regulate AI
text: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman testifies before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee on May 16, 2023. He proposes licensing or registration for AI models above a capability threshold, plus safety testing. Fellow witness Gary Marcus warns against a "trust us" approach from tech companies.
why: An AI company leader asked Congress for rules; Gary Marcus and Bruce Yandle questioned industry's role in them.

source.label: U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee, "Oversight of A.I.: Rules for Artificial Intelligence" hearing page (May 16, 2023)

image.credit: Office of the Prime Minister of Japan, CC BY 4.0
image.alt: Sam Altman at the Prime Minister's Residence in Tokyo, February 2025.

title: New York City requires audits of hiring AI
text: New York City begins enforcing Local Law 144. Employers that use automated tools to screen job applicants must have the tools checked for bias each year and post a summary of the results.
why: It was one of the first U.S. laws to require testing AI used in hiring.

source.label: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, "Automated Employment Decision Tools"

title: Bill Gates: AI risks manageable, expertise soon free
text: In a July 2023 blog post, Bill Gates wrote that AI's risks are real but manageable, as with past technologies. In February 2025 he told Jimmy Fallon that within a decade AI would make great medical advice and tutoring "free, commonplace."
why: Bill Gates's statements about AI and the future of doctors and teachers drew public responses from Randi Weingarten and David Leslie.

source.label: CNBC Make It, Tom Huddleston Jr., "Bill Gates: Within 10 years, AI will replace many doctors and teachers" (Mar. 26, 2025)

title: China's Cyberspace Administration issues generative AI rules
text: On July 13, 2023, the Cyberspace Administration of China and six other agencies publish interim measures for generative AI services, effective August 15. Public-facing services must uphold "core socialist values" and, if they can sway public opinion, pass security reviews and register algorithms.
why: China required generative AI services to follow content rules and, in some cases, to pass security reviews.

source.label: CNN, "China takes major step in regulating generative AI services like ChatGPT" (July 14, 2023)

title: Blumenthal and Hawley propose a bipartisan AI framework
text: On September 8, 2023, Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) release a framework for AI legislation. The framework includes an independent oversight body that would license advanced models, legal liability for harms, and limits on AI involving children.
why: A Democrat and a Republican agreed on licensing rules; IBM and Google argued against a new oversight office.

source.label: Sen. Richard Blumenthal, press release, "Blumenthal & Hawley Announce Bipartisan Framework on Artificial Intelligence Legislation" (Sept. 8, 2023)

title: Schumer opens the Senate's AI Insight Forums
text: On September 13, 2023, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) opens closed-door AI Insight Forums, planned with Senators Rounds, Young and Heinrich. Musk, Zuckerberg, Altman, union leaders and researchers attend. Hawley (R-Mo.) skips it, calling it a "giant cocktail party" for Big Tech.
why: A 2024 roadmap sought $32 billion for AI research; Alondra Nelson said it put innovation before regulation.

source.label: Senate Democrats, "Majority Leader Schumer Opening Remarks for the Senate's Inaugural AI Insight Forum" (Sept. 13, 2023)

image.credit: U.S. Senate Photographic Studio/Jeff McEvoy, public domain
image.alt: Official U.S. Senate portrait of Chuck Schumer, 2017.

title: Hollywood writers and actors win AI rules
text: After long strikes, the Writers Guild reaches a deal that bars AI from writing or rewriting scripts and bars studios from requiring writers to use it. In December, actors in SAG-AFTRA approve a contract requiring consent and pay for digital replicas.
why: Workers used union contracts to set rules for AI before most laws existed.

source.label: Writers Guild of America, "Summary of the 2023 WGA MBA"

image.alt: A striking writer on a picket line holds a sign that reads "A.I.'s not taking your dumb notes!"

title: Robin Williams's daughter objects to AI recreations
text: In October 2023, during the actors' strike, Zelda Williams posted on Instagram that AI had been used to make her father's voice say anything people liked. In October 2025 she asked people to stop sending her AI videos of him.
why: The actors' deal approved that November requires informed consent and pay for digital replicas.

source.label: Fortune, "Zelda Williams says 'stop sending me AI videos of Dad'" (Oct. 8, 2025)

title: U.S. executive order on AI, later revoked
text: President Biden signs Executive Order 14110 on safe and trustworthy AI, which requires developers of the most powerful models to share safety test results with the government. President Trump revokes it on January 20, 2025.
why: It shows how quickly national AI policy can change between administrations.

source.label: American Presidency Project, Executive Order 14148 (revokes EO 14110)

image.credit: Adam Schultz (The White House), Public domain
image.alt: President Joe Biden signs an executive order on artificial intelligence in the East Room of the White House, October 30, 2023.

title: Rishi Sunak hosts the Bletchley AI Safety Summit
text: British Prime Minister Rishi Sunak hosts the first AI Safety Summit at Bletchley Park on November 1 and 2, 2023. Twenty-eight countries and the EU, including the United States and China, sign the Bletchley Declaration on risks from frontier AI.
why: Sunak called it "a landmark achievement"; over 100 organizations wrote that affected workers and communities were marginalized.

source.label: GOV.UK, "The Bletchley Declaration by Countries Attending the AI Safety Summit, 1-2 November 2023"

image.credit: Simon Walker / Prime Minister's Office, Open Government Licence v3.0
image.alt: Official portrait of Prime Minister Rishi Sunak at 10 Downing Street, November 2022.

title: Beatles finish "Now and Then" with machine learning
text: The Beatles release "Now and Then" on November 2, 2023. Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr finish it from a 1970s John Lennon demo, using machine learning to separate Lennon's voice from the piano on the original cassette.
why: It is a mainstream example of AI used to restore an old recording.

source.label: The Associated Press via Fortune, "You can now listen to the final Beatles song, which wouldn't exist without AI" (Nov. 2, 2023)

title: New York proposes Empire AI
text: Governor Kathy Hochul proposes Empire AI, a shared AI computing center at the University at Buffalo for New York research universities, with SUNY and CUNY among its founding members. The state budget funded it in April 2024.
why: It is intended to give SUNY researchers access to large-scale computing.

source.label: Office of the Governor (Jan. 8, 2024), Empire AI Consortium announcement

title: Wole Talabi publishes Convergence Problems
text: Wole Talabi's story collection Convergence Problems is released in February 2024. Its 16 stories, mostly set in Nigeria, include "Debut," in which two AI nodes make art for other AIs, and other tales of technology and daily life.
why: It offers an Africanfuturist view of AI and technology from a Nigerian engineer and author.

source.label: Kirkus Reviews, "Convergence Problems" by Wole Talabi (release date Feb. 13, 2024)

title: Elon Musk sues OpenAI over its nonprofit mission
text: On February 29, 2024, Elon Musk, an OpenAI co-founder, sues OpenAI, Sam Altman and Greg Brockman, saying they abandoned its nonprofit, open mission for profit. OpenAI disputes this. In May 2026 an advisory jury finds he sued too late, and the judge dismisses the case.
why: The case aired disputes over OpenAI adding a for-profit business to its nonprofit; Musk says he will appeal.

source.label: NPR, Juliana Kim, "Elon Musk sues OpenAI for violating guiding principles in favor of profit" (Mar. 1, 2024)

title: Scarlett Johansson objects to OpenAI's Sky voice
text: On May 20, 2024, actor Scarlett Johansson says OpenAI's ChatGPT voice "Sky" sounds "eerily similar" to hers, after she declined Sam Altman's offer to license her voice. OpenAI pauses Sky, saying a different actress voiced it and resemblance was never intended.
why: Jyh-An Lee and Xuan Sun used the dispute to compare how laws protect a voice from AI cloning.

source.label: NPR, Bobby Allyn, "Scarlett Johansson says she is 'shocked, angered' over new ChatGPT voice" (May 20, 2024)

image.alt: Scarlett Johansson at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival.

title: The EU adopts the AI Act
text: The Council of the European Union gives final approval to the AI Act, after the European Parliament passed it in March. The law sorts AI uses by risk, bans some uses, and sets stricter rules for high-risk systems.
why: It is one of the first broad AI laws from a major government, and its rules apply in stages.

source.label: Council of the EU, "Artificial intelligence act: timeline"

image.credit: Publications Office of the European Union, Public domain
image.alt: The first page of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, as published in the Official Journal of the European Union on 12 July 2024.

title: Pope Francis addresses G7 leaders on AI
text: On June 14, 2024, Pope Francis becomes the first pope to address a G7 summit, at Giorgia Meloni's invitation. He asks leaders to keep decisions in human hands and ban lethal autonomous weapons. In their statement, the leaders back "responsible" military use of AI.
why: A religious leader joined government debates on AI, framing it as a question of human dignity.

source.label: Vatican, Address of Pope Francis to the G7 session on artificial intelligence, Borgo Egnazia (June 14, 2024)

image.credit: Korea.net / Korean Culture and Information Service (Jeon Han), CC BY-SA 2.0
image.alt: Pope Francis at Haemi Castle, South Korea, August 2014.

title: Sutskever launches Safe Superintelligence Inc.
text: In June 2024, former OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever launched Safe Superintelligence Inc. (SSI). The company said it has one goal and one product: a safe superintelligence. It has offices in Palo Alto and Tel Aviv.
why: It put "superintelligence" in a company name and called building a safe one "the most important technical problem of our time."

source.label: Safe Superintelligence Inc., company page

title: Academic publishers license research to AI companies
text: Taylor & Francis gave Microsoft access to its authors' research for AI, in a deal worth $10 million in the first year. Wiley said it expected $44 million from AI deals and confirmed authors could not opt out.
why: It raised questions about who controls, and who benefits from, scholarly work used to train AI.

source.label: The Bookseller, Aug. 30, 2024 (via infoDOCKET)

reading: Taylor & Francis authors said they had not been told about the Microsoft deal, had no option to opt out, and were not receiving extra payment.
musing: Publishers are selling access to work that authors wrote and worked on, that taxpayers supported, to AI companies. Authors often do that work for free in the pursuit of tenure and promotion, and then the publishers turn around and sell the work back to universities at a premium through the library. Meanwhile, people worry about putting an article into a chatbot to make an accessible PDF for their students because of the copyright implications. And I think, wow! What a racket.

title: Reasoning models work in steps
text: OpenAI releases o1-preview, a model trained to work through a problem in a long chain of steps before it answers. Such models do better on many math and coding tests but take longer to answer.
why: Giving a model more time on each answer became a new way to improve AI.

source.label: OpenAI, "Learning to reason with LLMs" (Sept. 12, 2024)

title: UB to lead $10 million AI literacy center
text: The University at Buffalo announces a $10 million U.S. Department of Education grant on September 19, 2024, for the Center for Early Literacy and Responsible AI. Its AI Reading Enhancer is meant to generate personalized texts and give real-time reading support to K-2 students.
why: A SUNY center will build AI reading support for young children.

source.label: UB News Center, "UB awarded $10 million grant to lead new national center on early literacy and responsible AI" (Sept. 19, 2024)

title: Chris Sanders adapts Peter Brown's The Wild Robot
text: Chris Sanders's DreamWorks film The Wild Robot adapts Peter Brown's 2016 book. A robot, Roz, washes up on an island, learns the animals' language and raises an orphaned gosling. It opened in the U.S. on September 27, 2024.
why: A children's story in which a machine learns care by raising a young animal.

source.label: The Encyclopedia of Science Fiction, "Wild Robot, The"

title: Gavin Newsom vetoes California's SB 1047 AI bill
text: On September 29, 2024, California Governor Gavin Newsom vetoes SB 1047, which would have required safety measures from developers of the largest AI models. He says it could give "a false sense of security." In 2025 he signs SB 53, a frontier AI transparency law.
why: Author Scott Wiener said the veto leaves companies without binding restrictions; OpenAI, Andreessen Horowitz and others opposed it.

source.label: Office of the Governor of California, SB 1047 veto message (Sept. 29, 2024)

image.credit: Charles Ommanney, Office of the Governor of California, public domain
image.alt: Official portrait of California Governor Gavin Newsom, 2026.

title: Nobel Prizes honor AI research
text: The physics prize goes to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for work that enables machine learning with artificial neural networks. The next day, the chemistry prize honors David Baker for computational protein design, and Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction.
why: Nobel committees honored AI methods and their use in science.

source.label: NobelPrize.org, "Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2024"

image.alt: Geoffrey Hinton and John Hopfield at the 2024 Nobel Lectures.

title: 43North awards $1 million to two AI startups
text: On October 10, 2024, 43North names five $1 million winners, including two AI companies. HeronAI makes a reporting tool for accounting firms. Spiky.ai coaches sales teams in real time. Both are Massachusetts startups, and Spiky is moving to Buffalo.
why: One of the two AI winners, Spiky.ai, is moving to Buffalo.

source.label: Office of the Governor (Oct. 10, 2024), 43North winners announcement

image.alt: Shea's Performing Arts Center in Buffalo, New York, December 2024. The 2024 43North finals were held at Shea's.

title: Families sue Character.AI and OpenAI over teen deaths
text: In October 2024, Megan Garcia sued Character.AI after her 14-year-old son's suicide. In August 2025, 16-year-old Adam Raine's parents sued OpenAI. OpenAI added parental controls; Character.AI ended open-ended chats for minors and agreed to settle in January 2026.
why: Courts and lawmakers are testing who is responsible for chatbot safety. In the US, call or text 988 for help.

source.label: CNN, Clare Duffy, "Character.AI and Google agree to settle lawsuits over teen mental health harms and suicides" (Jan. 7, 2026), via KTVZ

title: Wallace & Gromit's smart gnome, Norbot
text: Aardman's Vengeance Most Fowl premieres on BBC One and BBC iPlayer, then on Netflix outside the UK. Wallace invents Norbot, a smart garden gnome built for chores. When garden goods go missing, Wallace and Norbot are the main suspects.
why: The story raises the question of who is responsible when a smart device is suspected of a crime.

source.label: Aardman, "Watch the trailers for Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl"

title: SUNY adds AI to information literacy
text: SUNY announces that, starting with students entering in fall 2026, the general education information literacy requirement will include recognizing and ethically using AI. The SUNY Board of Trustees approved the change.
why: It puts learning about AI into the general education requirements for SUNY students, including at Fredonia.

source.label: SUNY press release (Jan. 7, 2025)

image.alt: Daniel A. Reed Library at SUNY Fredonia, seen from the southeast in April 2020.

title: Nnedi Okorafor publishes Death of the Author
text: Nnedi Okorafor's novel Death of the Author is released in January 2025. A Nigerian American writer pens a story of rusted robots, in which a humanoid robot and a bodiless AI challenge tribalism in robot society.
why: The novel won a Locus Award as best sf novel, according to the Encyclopedia of Science Fiction.

source.label: Kirkus Reviews, "Death of the Author" by Nnedi Okorafor (release date Jan. 14, 2025)

title: Trump, OpenAI, SoftBank, Oracle announce Stargate
text: At the White House on January 21, 2025, President Trump joined leaders of OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle to announce Stargate. They said it would invest up to $500 billion in U.S. AI data centers, starting with $100 billion.
why: It was announced at the White House; the next day Elon Musk said the partners did not have the money, and Sam Altman replied that Musk was wrong.

source.label: Al Jazeera, "Trump announces $500bn 'Stargate' venture to build up AI infrastructure" (Jan. 22, 2025)

title: AI agents start using computers
text: OpenAI releases Operator, an agent that uses a web browser to fill in forms and finish tasks for a person. Anthropic had released a similar computer-use feature in October 2024. Early tests found these agents still made mistakes.
why: AI began acting on the web for people, which raises new safety and privacy questions.

source.label: MIT Technology Review (Jan. 23, 2025)

title: Karpathy coins "vibe coding"
text: AI researcher Andrej Karpathy posts about "vibe coding": describing what you want to an AI tool and accepting the code it writes without studying it. Collins Dictionary named it its 2025 Word of the Year.
why: It named a new habit, and a new worry about code nobody has checked.

source.label: Collins Dictionary, "Collins Word of the Year 2025"

image.credit: Screenshot of ChatGPT output, Public domain
image.alt: A screenshot of ChatGPT writing a JavaScript function to shuffle a deck of cards after a plain-language request.

title: xAI edits Grok after answers about Musk, Trump
text: Over a weekend in February 2025, users found that xAI's chatbot Grok 3, asked who spreads the most misinformation on X, had been told not to mention Trump or Musk. xAI's engineering lead said an employee made the change and it was reversed.
why: It is one reported case of a chatbot's instructions being changed; a July 2025 executive order later set requirements for the models federal agencies buy.

source.label: TechCrunch (Kyle Wiggers), "Grok 3 appears to have briefly censored unflattering mentions of Trump and Musk" (Feb. 23, 2025)

title: Court rules AI alone cannot be an author
text: A U.S. federal appeals court agrees with the Copyright Office that a work made by an AI system alone cannot be registered, because copyright law requires a human author. The ruling left open how much human input AI-assisted work needs.
why: It matters for students and artists who use AI in creative work.

source.label: U.S. Court of Appeals, D.C. Circuit, Thaler v. Perlmutter, No. 23-5233

title: AI Futures Project forecasts superintelligence by 2027
text: In April 2025, Daniel Kokotajlo and four co-authors published AI 2027, a scenario in which superintelligent AI arrives by December 2027. It offers a "race" ending and a "slowdown" ending. A November 2025 note said their median forecasts were longer.
why: Coverage in The New York Times and elsewhere spread the forecast; skeptics say AI will change society gradually.

source.label: AI Futures Project, "AI 2027" (Apr. 3, 2025; note added Nov. 22, 2025)

title: UAlbany launches an AI and Society College
text: The University at Albany launches an Artificial Intelligence & Society College and research center on April 4, 2025. It grows out of AI Plus, begun in 2022, and brings AI coursework to all nine schools and colleges. The state announced $2.4 million over three years.
why: It is one SUNY campus's plan to bring AI coursework to all nine of its schools and colleges.

source.label: University at Albany News Center, "UAlbany Launches New AI & Society College, Research Center" (Apr. 4, 2025)

image.alt: The Academic Podium of the University at Albany's Uptown Campus.

title: UB creates a Department of AI and Society
text: The University at Buffalo announces a Department of AI and Society on April 7, 2025, with $5 million from Governor Hochul to open that fall. In August, the governor announced seven AI-focused bachelor's degrees and two minors, including AI ethics.
why: It adds AI-focused degrees at a SUNY campus, paired with study of AI's effects on society.

source.label: UB News Center, "UB to launch new academic department focusing on AI and society" (Apr. 7, 2025)

image.alt: Capen Hall on the University at Buffalo North Campus, December 2008.

title: Trump and White House post AI-made images
text: Trump's Truth Social account and official White House accounts have posted AI-made images and videos, including one of Trump as the pope on May 2, 2025. Officials call them memes or satire. Critics say they erode trust in government information.
why: Official government accounts have posted AI-made images, and officials and critics describe them differently.

source.label: PBS NewsHour, "Trump's use of AI images further erodes public trust, experts say" (Jan. 27, 2026)

title: Pope Leo XIV links his name to AI
text: On May 10, 2025, two days after his election, Pope Leo XIV tells cardinals he chose his name mainly because Leo XIII addressed the first industrial revolution, and AI now poses "new challenges for the defence of human dignity, justice and labour."
why: He made AI a theme of his papacy, issuing Magnifica Humanitas, an encyclical on AI, in May 2026.

source.label: Vatican, Address of Pope Leo XIV to the College of Cardinals (May 10, 2025)

image.credit: Edgar Beltrán, The Pillar, CC BY-SA 4.0
image.alt: Pope Leo XIV at a meeting with the media, May 12, 2025.

title: Karen Hao's Empire of AI
text: Journalist Karen Hao publishes Empire of AI, a book about OpenAI. She argues that a few AI companies act like empires, drawing on other people's data, low-paid labor, energy and water.
why: It added to public debate about the labor and environmental effects of AI.

source.label: Penguin Random House, Empire of AI by Karen Hao

image.alt: Journalist Karen Hao speaking at a 2025 author talk for Empire of AI at Politics and Prose bookstore.

title: 404 Media, Illinois audit find federal Flock searches
text: Flock Safety sells AI-enabled license plate cameras used in more than 4,000 US communities. In May 2025, 404 Media reported over 4,000 police searches tied to immigration. In August, an Illinois audit found federal border agents had accessed Illinois data; Flock paused federal pilots.
why: Cameras bought by one town can feed searches by agencies far away, including immigration enforcement.

source.label: Associated Press, John O'Connor, "License plate camera company halts cooperation with federal agencies among investigation concerns" (Aug. 26, 2025), via ABC7

title: MIT Media Lab records EEG during ChatGPT essays
text: In June 2025, Nataliya Kosmyna's team at the MIT Media Lab posted a preprint. Of 54 participants writing essays, those using ChatGPT showed the weakest brain connectivity on EEG and felt least ownership of their essays. The paper was not yet peer reviewed.
why: Headlines said AI makes people dumb; the authors asked reporters not to say that.

source.label: Kosmyna et al., "Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task," arXiv:2506.08872 (v1 June 10, 2025)

title: Altman blogs that "the takeoff has started"
text: On June 10, 2025, OpenAI chief Sam Altman posted "The Gentle Singularity." He wrote that AI is past "the event horizon," said systems with novel insights are likely in 2026, and called for superintelligence that is cheap, widely available and not too concentrated.
why: Sam Altman wrote that "the takeoff has started," and Gary Marcus has criticized OpenAI's promises as harder to keep.

source.label: Sam Altman, "The Gentle Singularity" (blog, June 10, 2025)

title: Zuckerberg launches Meta Superintelligence Labs
text: On June 30, 2025, Mark Zuckerberg told Meta staff that the company was forming Meta Superintelligence Labs, led by Alexandr Wang. On July 30 he published an essay on "personal superintelligence" and said Meta would be careful about what it open sources.
why: Meta named a new lab after "superintelligence," and Zuckerberg wrote about "personal superintelligence."

source.label: CNBC via NBC New York, "Mark Zuckerberg announces creation of Meta Superintelligence Labs, read the memo" (June 30, 2025)

title: Senate votes 99-1 to drop state AI ban
text: The House version of the 2025 budget bill would have barred states from regulating AI for 10 years. On July 1, 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to remove that ban. According to Sen. Edward Markey, 17 Republican governors and 40 attorneys general had objected.
why: It left states free to write their own AI rules, and the question of one national standard came back in December 2025.

source.label: States Newsroom (Paige Gross), "Senate votes 99-1 to remove AI moratorium from megabill" (July 1, 2025)

title: Shelby County permits xAI turbines; NAACP appeals
text: On July 2, 2025, Shelby County's health department permitted 15 gas turbines at xAI's Colossus data center in Memphis. The NAACP and Southern Environmental Law Center say xAI ran at least 35 without permits, and appealed. xAI says its operations comply with all applicable laws.
why: Critics say the permit overlooked earlier unpermitted turbines. The NAACP sued xAI in April 2026 over its Mississippi turbines.

source.label: Inside Climate News, "In South Memphis, Elon Musk's Colossus Operated Gas Turbines Without Appropriate Permits, Residents and Activists Claim" (July 17, 2025)

title: White House issues America's AI Action Plan
text: On July 23, 2025, the White House released America's AI Action Plan with three pillars: faster innovation, more infrastructure, and international leadership. Trump also signed executive orders on data centers, AI exports, and "woke AI" in federal purchasing.
why: It states the aim of "global dominance" in AI, and supporters and critics read its approach to rules very differently.

source.label: The White House, America's AI Action Plan (July 2025)

title: Tucson council rejects Amazon-linked Project Blue data center
text: On August 6, 2025, the Tucson City Council voted unanimously to end talks on Project Blue, a data center tied to Amazon, after residents raised water and power concerns. The developer said the project would be net water positive. It later advanced in Pima County.
why: Tucson moved to limit large water users. The project went ahead in Pima County, and the state approved its wells.

source.label: AZ Luminaria, "Tucson City Council rejects Project Blue data center amid intense community pressure" (Aug. 6, 2025)

title: Seneca Nation challenges STAMP data center approvals
text: In September 2025, a Genesee County development agency withdrew approvals for a data center at the STAMP site after the Tonawanda Seneca Nation and the Sierra Club sued. The Nation cites risks to water and wells. The agency says a larger plan would add jobs.
why: In July 2026 a New York pause on large data center permits appeared to halt the larger plan.

source.label: WXXI News, "Genesee County STAMP site data center on hold as expansion gets pursued" (Sept. 18, 2025)

title: Bernie Sanders warns of AI job losses
text: On October 6, 2025, Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) releases a HELP Committee minority staff report estimating AI and automation could replace nearly 100 million U.S. jobs in ten years. The estimate is based on a ChatGPT analysis. He proposes a robot tax and a 32-hour week.
why: James Pethokoukis, Emily Bender and Alex Hanna criticized the report's use of ChatGPT to estimate job losses.

source.label: Senate HELP Committee minority staff (Ranking Member Bernard Sanders), "The Big Tech Oligarchs' War Against Workers" (Oct. 6, 2025)

image.alt: Senator Bernie Sanders speaking at Stanford University about the future of AI, February 2026.

title: Buffalo News reports rise in AI-generated Bills posts
text: The Buffalo News reports on October 21, 2025 that AI-generated social media posts about the Bills are on the rise. A caption describes one false post claiming Josh Allen sent six planes of aid to Texas flood victims.
why: It is a local report on AI-generated social media posts aimed at football fans.

source.label: The Buffalo News, "AI-generated posts about the Buffalo Bills are on the rise. Here's why" (Katherine Fitzgerald, Oct. 21, 2025)

title: Future of Life Institute urges superintelligence ban
text: On October 22, 2025, the Future of Life Institute released a statement calling for a ban on developing superintelligence until there is broad scientific agreement it can be done safely and strong public support. Hundreds of scientists, business leaders and public figures signed at launch.
why: Public figures across politics asked for limits on a goal that several tech companies are pursuing.

source.label: Future of Life Institute, Statement on Superintelligence

title: Trump signs Genesis Mission order for AI science
text: On November 24, 2025, Trump signed an order creating the Genesis Mission. The Energy Department and national labs will combine science data and supercomputers so AI can speed research in areas such as energy, materials and quantum science.
why: It is a named federal AI project that the White House compares to Apollo; House Science Committee Democrats criticized proposed cuts to science funding.

source.label: The White House, Fact Sheet: Genesis Mission (Nov. 24, 2025)

title: DeSantis proposes a Florida AI Bill of Rights
text: On December 4, 2025, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis (R) proposes an AI Bill of Rights: parental controls for chatbots, consent before AI uses a person's likeness, and privacy rules. The state Senate passes it in 2026; the House adjourns without taking it up.
why: A Republican governor pressed for state AI rules as President Trump sought to preempt them.

source.label: Executive Office of the Governor of Florida, "Governor Ron DeSantis Announces Proposal for Citizen Bill of Rights for Artificial Intelligence" (Dec. 4, 2025)

image.alt: Official portrait of Florida Governor Ron DeSantis.

title: Trump orders federal challenge to state AI laws
text: On December 11, 2025, Trump signed an order targeting state AI laws it calls "onerous." It sets up a Justice Department task force to challenge them and directs agencies to consider withholding some federal funds. It states that Congress should adopt one national standard.
why: Federal and state officials disagree over who may set AI rules.

source.label: The White House, "Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence" (Dec. 11, 2025)

title: New York passes the RAISE Act
text: Governor Hochul signs the RAISE Act. It requires developers of the largest, most advanced AI models to publish safety plans and report serious safety incidents to the state within 72 hours.
why: New York joined California in passing a safety law for the most advanced AI models.

source.label: Office of the Governor (Dec. 19, 2025)

title: Evanston, Austin and dozens more drop Flock cameras
text: Austin let its Flock contract lapse in June 2025, and Evanston, Illinois, switched off 19 cameras that August. NPR counted at least 30 places that canceled or deactivated Flock by February 2026. Washington state limited plate-reader uses in March 2026.
why: Residents and officials weighed police claims of solved crimes against privacy and immigration concerns, in public meetings nationwide.

source.label: NPR, Jude Joffe-Block, "Why some cities are ditching their Flock license plate readers" (Feb. 17, 2026), via WLRN

title: Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders propose data center moratorium
text: On March 25, 2026, Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced a bill to pause new U.S. data centers until Congress sets safeguards, including no higher electricity prices and no harm to communities or the environment. Opponents include Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) and the Data Center Coalition.
why: It brought local worries about power bills, water and pollution to Congress, though the AP calls it unlikely to advance.

source.label: Sen. Bernie Sanders, press release "Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez Announce AI Data Center Moratorium Act" (Mar. 25, 2026)

image.credit: Franmarie Metzler, U.S. House Office of Photography, public domain
image.alt: Official portrait of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

title: Professors bring back blue books and oral exams
text: After ChatGPT, some professors moved tests back into the classroom. The Wall Street Journal reported blue book sales up nearly 50% at the University of Florida in 2025. By 2026, faculty at Cornell, Penn and NYU were giving oral exams.
why: Supporters say in-person tests are the clearest way to know the work is the student's own; critics say timed, watched writing is poor teaching and stresses anxious students.

source.label: Associated Press, "Perfect homework, blank stares: Why colleges are turning to oral exams to combat AI" (Apr. 22, 2026), via WTOP

title: Maine Governor Mills vetoes data center moratorium
text: On April 24, 2026, Maine Governor Janet Mills vetoed LD 307, which would have been the first statewide data center moratorium. It would have paused projects over 20 megawatts until November 2027. Mills wanted an exemption for a $550 million project in Jay.
why: The House failed to override, 72 to 65. Mills instead created a 15-member council to study data center impacts.

source.label: Office of Governor Janet Mills, "Governor Mills Announces Decision on LD 307" (Apr. 24, 2026)

image.alt: The Maine State House in Augusta, completed in 1832.

title: SUNY adopts a systemwide AI policy
text: SUNY's systemwide Artificial Intelligence Policy takes effect. Every campus, including Fredonia, must adopt or update its own AI guidelines by December 31, 2026, covering roles, training on responsible use, and safeguards when buying AI tools.
why: It sets the rules that Fredonia's own AI guidelines must follow.

source.label: SUNY Policies and Procedures, Systemwide Artificial Intelligence Policy (Doc. 6904)

title: Ocasio-Cortez asks EPA about data center water quality
text: On May 20, 2026, at a House hearing, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez held up two jars of well water she said came from near a Meta data center campus in Georgia. She asked EPA official Jessica Kramer about testing. Kramer said she would look into it.
why: Meta disputes that its construction caused the problem. EPA later said neither it nor Georgia regulates private wells.

source.label: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, press release with remarks as delivered (May 20, 2026)

title: Google pledges to replenish more water by 2030
text: On June 3, 2026, Google said it will replenish more water than it consumes at its sites by 2030. It reported replenishing over 7 billion gallons in 2025 and said it will choose air cooling or recycled water in high-risk watersheds.
why: Ceres asked how the projects will measurably protect water supplies in water-stressed regions.

source.label: Google, "Google's water stewardship commitments for local communities" (June 3, 2026)

title: Governor Hochul orders pause on large data centers
text: On July 14, 2026, New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order pausing state environmental permits for data centers using 50 megawatts or more, for up to a year, while the state studies energy, water and community effects.
why: Hochul has until year-end to sign, veto or amend the Legislature's stricter 20-megawatt bill.

source.label: New York Public News Network via WSKG, "Hochul draws cheers, jeers over statewide data center moratorium" (July 14, 2026)

title: Hochul announces Empire AI Beta online at UB
text: On August 5, 2026, Governor Kathy Hochul announces that Empire AI Beta, a $40 million NVIDIA supercomputer at the University at Buffalo, is fully online. It has 11 times the AI training capacity of the 2024 Alpha system, and over 300 projects are queued.
why: It gives SUNY and other New York researchers large-scale AI computing, a goal first proposed in January 2024.

source.label: Office of the Governor (Aug. 5, 2026), Empire AI Beta fully online

image.alt: The skyline of the Buffalo Niagara Medical Campus, November 2019. Empire AI Beta is housed at a UB center on the medical campus.

title: Bills choose AiFi checkout-free stands for stadium
text: In an August 10, 2026 interview, Bills IT project director Shaun Handley said the new Highmark Stadium's concession stands will use checkout-free technology from AiFi, described in a PayPal case study as "spatial AI technology." The stadium also adds walk-through security scanners.
why: A local team plans checkout-free stands, and its IT project director cited past halftime concession problems.

source.label: Stadium Tech Report, "Shaun Handley discusses how tech upgrades will make Bills fans happy at the new Highmark Stadium" (Aug. 10, 2026)

image.alt: Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, viewed from the west, May 2026.

title: Georgia families sue Meta over well water
text: On August 31, 2026, families near Meta's data center in Newton County, Georgia, sued in Gwinnett County court. They say clearing, blasting and excavation clouded their well water with silt. Meta says its study found groundwater flows away from their homes.
why: Rep. Ocasio-Cortez raised it in May. EPA later said neither it nor Georgia regulates private wells.

source.label: Atlanta Journal-Constitution, "Georgia families sue Meta, accuse its data center of tainting their water" (Sept. 1, 2026)

title: TypeSafe AI releases Jev in early access
text: On September 15, 2026, TypeSafe AI released Jev in early access. The company says Jev returns typed answers with probabilities to software, in 70 to 500 milliseconds.
why: The company supplied the speed figure. KDnuggets' Abid Ali Awan writes that Jev's answers can still be wrong.

source.label: TypeSafe AI blog, Diogo Almeida, "Introducing System One Models & Jev" (Sep. 15, 2026)

title: Trump orders agencies to say "Super Intelligence"
text: On September 29, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14434. It directs federal agencies to use "Super Intelligence" and "SI" instead of "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" in non-statutory documents. Earlier documents and laws stay unchanged. Six tech leaders also signed the Accord on Super Intelligence, which Mashable reports has no penalties.
why: It renames AI in federal documents without changing any law, and some tech leaders kept saying AI.

source.label: The White House, "Inaugurating The Era Of Super Intelligence" (EO 14434, Sept. 29, 2026)
